12. There has been an increase of Rs. 1.90 crorcs this year, as against the revised estimates of the 
last year, which, in view of price esclation, is negligible. Therefore, the Committee feels that allocation 
for ASI should be adeq uately increase d because a large number of monument s are in dilapidated 
conditions and need urg ent repairs and a great number of monument s and sites remain unidentified 
and unprotected. Out of arou nd 8,000 monuments, about 3,500 are cent rally protecte d. The Committee 
expresses its concern over the fact that even the centrally prot ected monuments do not have proper 
maintenance and foolpr oof protectioq. Cases of larcen y of artefacts, idols etc. have been occuring from 
time to time. During the course of evidence the Committee came to know that the number of staff 
engaged in preservations and maintenance of monuments is so small that the ratio works out to 11h 
staff per monument. Therefore, the Committee recommen ds that staff st rength of the ASI engage d for 
protection and preservation of monuments be adequa tely increased and all other necessary measures be 
taken to check the increasing menace of pilferage. Some amount from the proposed National Cultural 
Fund may also be utilised for the purpo se. 
The Committee is also of the view that, as envisaged in the Eigh th Plan documen t related to the 
Department of Cultur e, volunta ry organ isations should be attracted and encouraged to take up the task 
of preservation and protection of monu.ments. 
13. Even after one hundred and twenty five years of its existence, ASI has not been able to cover 
all parts of the country as far as excavation and exploration of ancient historical sites are concerned. 
Nor it has been able to decipher all the inscriptions. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the 
network of ASI sho uld ha ve been extensively expanded and enlarged. It should also be well equipped. 
The scheme of village to village survev should also be undertaken and expanded. 
Anthropological Survey of India 
14. Researches in anthropology and allied disciplines and study of customs and traditions are 
some of the major functions undertaken by the Anthropological Survey of India. In the Eighth Five 
Year Plan document it was proposed to salvage and document those specimens of the tribal and folk 
art which face the threat of extinction. It was also proposed to study inherent socio-religious 
disabilities of the tribals, nature of transformation and mobilisation of their special skills in arts, dance 
and music and mastery over musical instruments. But, no follow-up action on these lines is found in 
the Annual Plans of the Department. Therefore, the Committee urges upon the Government to pursue 
vigorously those objectives. Reasons for decrease in the plan allocation of Rs. 140.00 lakhs from Rs. 
150.00 lakhs (Plan Expenditure Revised) of the year 1993;94 arc not tenable . Hence the Committee 
recommends that the provision shou ld be incr eased. Study and research in the field of conservation of 
environment, welfare of women and children, nutritional status of Indian population, etc. have also 
been added to its activ~ties, recently. 

15. In keeping with its aims and objectives, the Anthropological Survey of India took up a 
national project called 'People of Indi a' to analyse Indian population on the basis of bio-cultural 
variables and socio-cultural determinents like marriage, kinship, region, language etc. Out of the 
proposed 43 volumes of the prestigious National Project 'People of India'- three under national and 
two under State ser ies have so far been published. The remaining work should be expedited. 
Museums 
16. Museums play a vital role in the preservation of documents and objects of cultural antiquity. 
In this field, at present, there are ten premier institutions under Govt. of India, including the 
National Reserach Laboratory for Conservation of Cultural property located at Lucknow. Out of the 
ten institutions, three each are located at New Delhi and Calcutta and one each at Lucknow, 
Allahabad, Hyderabad and Bombay, all situated in major cities. To provide representation to cultural 
aspects of other states of Indian Union, a new scheme for Promotion and Strengthening of Regional 
and Local Museums has been mooted and is envisaged to be operationlised during the Eighth Five 
Year Plan period. Govt. is also providing assistance for opening private museums. Govt. proposes to 
intensify this scheme through a Committee which will look after them. But for this well conceived 
scheme a meagre amount of Rs. 10 lakhs has been provided for the year 1994-95. There has been no 
change in the allocations for the last three years. In such a situation the Committee wonders how the 
scheme contemplated for the Eighth Plan could be implemented within the time-frame with this 
insignificant budget allocation. As the Eighth Five Year Plan is left with only two financial years, the 
Committee strongly recommends enhancement of financial allocation to speed up the implementation of 
the scheme. 
National Council of Science Museums (NCSM), Calcutta 
17. It is an autonomous organisation engaged primarily in the task of popularising science and 
technology among the students in particular and the mas~es in general through a variety of interactive 
and innovative programmes and activities like science exhibitions, school centres, portable 
planetarium and national science seminars etc. and setting up of a Science City in Calcutta, is the 
highlight of the activities of the National Council of Science Museums. In the Eighth Plan document it 
was proposed to create 1000 science centres to reach the common man, five new regional centres, 20 
district science centres and 203 school science centres in the under privileged rural schools, 20 new 
mobile science exhibition buses, a science train, etc. The total out lay for the 8th Plan period of Rs. 
4500.00 lakhs for these ambitious proposals is too littfe. Slight increase in the allocation for this year, 
as against the last year's Budget Estimates, of around Rs. 161 lakhs and of Rs. 111 lakhs in Revised 
Estimates may not be said to be adequate in view of the rising prices. The implementation of the 
scheme has made very little progress and should be speeded up. Therefore, the Committee recommends 
that additional grant be given for this scheme to increase scientific temper among the people. 
National Museum, New Delhi 
18. During 1994-95, the National Museum, New Delhi, proposes to organise exhibitions of 
Persian manuscripts in Teheran, an exhibition of Indian Art at Singapore and of miniature paintings 
at Tashkent. Apart from this, it is also proposed to introduce such new programmes as developing 
software for physically handicapped persons, lending consultancy services to the State and other 
museums, introduction of disc system for documentation of its huge collection, microfilming of 
manuscripts and computerisation of its library, etc. 
19. The provisions made for this year, as against last year, remain more or less the same. Plan 
provision has fallen from Rs. 200.00 lakhs to Rs. 190.00 lakhs and Non-Plan provisions has increased 
by only Rs. 7 lakhs in comparison to the Revised Estimates of the last year. Thus, there has been a 
decrease of Rs. 3 lakhs this year. The Committee is surprised to know as to how with this small 
allocation. It would be possible to achieve the targets set for this year. The Committee therefore, 
recomm ends that the allocation for National Museum be increased appropriately. 
Indian Museum, Calcutta 
20. The total provisions made this year for Indian Museum, Calcutta, arc less by 1.45 lakhs as 
agianst the Revised Estimates (both Plan and Non-Plan) of the last year. In this situation, apart from 

carrying out on-going functions the proposal to construct a new building for display of valuable 
artefacts may find itself in rough weather. It was also envisaged in the Eighth Plan document to set 
up new galler ies on textiles, folk arts, gems and jewelleries. Therefore, the Committee recommends 
that sufficient grant should be provided to the Museum so that these schemes are completed. 
Institutes and Organisations of Tibetan and Buddhist studies 
21. There are. four autonomous institutes, namely, the Central Institute of Higher Tibetan 
Studies, VaranasC the Central Institute of Buddhist Studies, Leh; the Sikkim Research Institute of 
Tibetology and the Library of Tibetan Works & Archives, Dharamsala, which are engaged in 
preservation and propagations of Tibetan culture and tradition, restoration of ancient Indian literature 
preserved in Tibetan language, imparting higher education in Buddhist philosophy and literature, etc. 
The Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, Varanasi, enjoys the status of a 'Deemed 
University'. The Committee while expressing its satisfaction over the encouragement given to these 
institutes feels that they should be allowed to pursue their academic interest without any extraneous 
influences. 
22. The Committee feels that due attention is not being paid in these institutes to promotion and 
development of Pali, one of ancient language of India and, therefore, recommends suitable steps in this 
regard. 
Libraries 
23. The Committee feels that the reading habi!s of the general masses are on the wane, partly 
owing to revolutionary changes in electronic media, partly due to the shift in social values titled more 
to materialism, and partly because of high prices of books. In this situation, libraries have to be 
opened on a large scale with even distribution in urban and rural areas. 
24. There arc six major libraries under the Department of Culture. The total budgetary provision 
(lOth Plan and Non -Plan) for the year 1994-95 under this .head is Rs. 13.36 crores a total increase of 
Rs. 2.38 crores in comparison to the Revised Estimates (Both Plan & Non Plan) of the last year. In 
view of the rising prices of books and other allied items, maintenance cost of buildings etc. this 
increase of Rs. 2.38 crores in not enough. 
25. The tendency of centralisation is perceptible in the scheme of libraries also. The Committee 
feels that suitable scheme be devised to spread the network of libraries to District Headquarters and 
small towns. There is also a need to Interlink the major libraries with computer network. It will 
facilitate the research scholars and other persons desiring any information sitting in one library to 
gather additional information from all the connected libraries. 
26. The Delhi Public Library, established in 1951 with the assistance of UNESCO to provide free 
library service to the citizens of Delhi , has also now developed into a Metropolitan Public Library. A 
major portion of its activities is located in the affluent localities of Delhi and the rural and 
underdeveloped areas are being neglected . Therefore, -the Committee, recommends that Govt. should 
take adequate steps to spread it~ network of libraries and reading rooms in the slum and 
underdeveloped ar~as of the National Capital. More and more mobile library vans should also be made 
available. In view of all these, the Committee recommends that the budget allocation for Delhi Public 
Library be enhanced appropriately. 
Raja Ram Mohan Roy Library Foundation, Calcutta 
27. Established in 1972, it is an autonomous organisation fully funded by the Deptt: of Culture. 
The · main aim of the library is to support and promote library services in the country. 
28. Increase in its budget provision this year is welcome. However, some Irregularities in the 
fuQctioning of the lib_rary have come to the notice of the Committee. Guidelines on book purchasing are 
not being adhered to and books are allegedly being purchased at higher r~tes than the market rates. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that these matters be looked Into. 

Rural Library Scheme 
29. The Committee is happy to note that the Department of Culture has decided to focus its 
attention on the rural populace by deciding to set up rural libraries in villages. A teacher from the 
local school is proposed to be made in-charge of the library which will, in the incipient,have around 
300 books. The Committee "is of the view that these libraries should also ~ave such books which may be 
used by neo-literates in the post-literacy stage. It is, undoubtedly a well conceived scheme and generous 
funds should be provided for it. The Committee recommends that this scheme be made a pilot project 
so that about five and half lakh villages could be covered within a stipulated time-frame. The 
Committee also recommends that separate allocation be made for individual states. In consultation with 
the Ministry of Rural Development, the assistance of Panchayats may be sought to ensure speedy and 
effective implementation of this scheme. The Committee also recommends that the modalities for the 
implementation of this scheme be worked out as early as possible so that the scheme implemented in 
right earnest. 
Akademies and National School of Drama 
I. Sahitya Akademi

1956 with the objective of working actively for development of literature and to foster and coordinate 
literary activities in all the Indian languages and to promote through them the cultural unity of the· 
country. To achieve these objectives, the Akademi is running programmes such as granting literary 
awards, translation and publication of books in different languages, etc. The Akademi also provides 
assistance to State Akademies. 
31. The Committee is not happy with the budgetary allocation made for the Akademi this year, 
which is only Rs. 57 lakhs more than the Revised Estimates of the last year :-

32. The Committee expresses its concern over the fact that a premier literary institution like the 
Sahitya Akademi is made ·to curtail its activities due to lack of funds. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends strongly that more resources be made available to the Sahitya Akademi and the arrear 
payments, if any, should also be released forthwith. The Akademi should bestow more attention on the 
development of regional languages, in addition to Hindi. 
II. Sangeet Natak Akademi 
33. The Sangeet Natak Akademi, which come into being in 1953, is a national institution engaged 
in promotion and preservation of performing arts, extending financial assistance to cultural institution 
for training and production, undertaking inter-state cultural exchange programmes etc. Although 
there is an increase of around Rs. 27 lakhs this year, as compared to the last year's Revised Estimates 
(both Plan and Non-Plan) this is negligible in view of the price escalation. The Committee is of the 
view that the outlay for the Akademi may be appropriately increased. 
III. Lalit Kala Akademi 
34. The Lalit Kala Akademi an apex institution in the field of art was established in 1954 for the 
promotion and development of paintings, graphics, sculpture, ceramics, etc. in the country. The major 
activities of the Akademi are to organise exhibitions (in and outside the country), artists' camps, 
bringing out art publications, and implementing cultural exchange programmes. 
35. The allocation for the Akademi this year has come down from Rs. 2.85 crores (Revised 
estimates) of the year 1993-94 to Rs. 2.40 crores. The Committee urges upon the Govt. to increase the 
allocation appropriately. 

National School of Drama 
36. The National School of Drama, established in 1959, is a premier institution devoted to 
imparting training in the field of theatre and to propagate dramatics in the country. Increase in this 
year's budgetary provisions for the institution from Rs. 266.65 lakhs to Rs. 285.00 lakhs is welcome. 
The National School of Drama proposes to set up regional centres, which is a welcome step, and the 
Committee desires that these regional centres should enjoy due autonomy in their functioning and not 
made mere branches of the National School of Drama, New Delhi. 
Promotion of Art & Culture 
37. A number of organisations and institutions are active in promoting and disseminating 
different types of art and cultural activities in various regions and zones of the country. A brief sketch 
of their activities, objectives vis-a-vis provisions thereof is given below:-
/. Centre for Cultural Resources & Training 
38. The Centre for Cultural Resources and Training, set up in 1979 with its headquarter in New 
Delhi, is doing a commendable job in the propagation of culture, especially among college and school 
students. One of the major activities of the Centre is to train inservice school teachers in the area of 
linkage between education and culture and to provide a cultural component in the curricula. The 
Centre also prepares audio-visuals and printed materials to be used in schools for cultural education. 
The centre also took over the scheme 'Cultural Talent Search Scholarship' from the Deptt. of Culture 
in 1982 under which 300 children in the age group of 10-14 years are awarded scholarships each year 
in various fields. 
39. The Centre has been entrusted with the task of interlinking culture with education, mass 
media and the scheme of the Deptt., bearing an identical nomenclature, has since been merged with 
the centre's scheme. 
40. The Committee is of the view that it is not practically feasible to cover whole country by the 
one and only Centre in New Delhi and hence feels the need to decentralise the activities of the Centre 
by opening sub-centres in various zones and regions. 
41. The provisions made for the Centre are not in consonance with the multifarious activities of the 
Centre. A comparative analysis of the allocation suggests that there has been a meagre increase of 
Rs. 20 lakhs in Plan and 0.65 lakhs in Non-Plan expenditure, as against the revised estimates of the last 
year. Since this is the only institution which is taking culture down to the general masses, students and 
teachers, the Committee recommends that more .resources should be allocated to the Centre, 
particularly keeping in view the Committee's recommendation for opening sub-Centres at various 
places. 
Zonal Cultural Centres 
42. At present, there are seven Zonal Cultural Centres which cover the entire country. The main 
functions of the Zonal Cultural Centres are to provide facilities for the creative development in the 
entire spectrum of culture, particularly in that of folk and tribal art. These centres are also 
implementing National Cultural Exchange Programmes, Republic Day folk dance festival and setting 
up Shilpgrams etc. For the year 1994-95 a sum of Rs. 200 lakhs has been earmarked for zonal cultural 
centres. During the year 1992-93 there was an under-utilisation of the approved outlay to the tune of 
about Rs. 175 lakhs, mainly because of the delay in allotment of land by Sta~ Government for setting 
up of Shilpgrams. The Committee, however, feels that such delays should be avoided so that funds are 
utilised in time. The Committee recommends that speedy progress be made in setting up Shilpgrams at 
the remaining six zonal cultural centres, particularly the one being set up at Thanjavur. The 
Committee also feels that centrewise allocation should also be reflected in the documents of the 
Department. 
43. Documentation and propagation of folk art constitute one of the main functions of Zonal 
Cultural Centres and as stated by the Secretary, Department of Culture, it is also one of the major 
thrust areas during this year. But the work being done in this regard cannot be said to be satisfactory. 
There is no indication as to how much money each Zonal Cultur al Centre spends on the propagation of 
the Jjving folk art forms at the grassroot level in villages where they are actually performed. Therefore, 

~he Committee is of the view that due emphasis of the Zonal .Cultural Centres should be on folk arts 
and necessary financial assistance should also be provided for the same. 
44. The Committee is constrained to note that the hopes generated at the time of establishment of 
Zonal Cultural Centres have not been fulfilled and realised. Because these centres are not pursuing the 
programmes and schemes fop which they were set up, therefore, the Committee recommends that the 
time has come for a high-powered Review Committee to be constituted to look into the working of the 
Zonal Cultural Centres. 
Dissemination of Tribal Folk Art & Culture 
45. Under this scheme, financial support is given to voluntary cultural organisations, institutions 
and individuals-both tribal and non-tribal for undertaking small duration projects of around one year 
for preservation and development of tribal folk art and culture, conduct of tribal cultural activities, 
including their festivals and festivities. This year, there has been an increase of Rs. 10 lakhs for this 
scheme. But the Committee is not happy with the working of the voluntary organisations/institutions 
in this field because it is found that the assistance does not percolate down to the folk artistes, 
although the Secretary, Department of Culture, has submitted before the Committee that Gqvern­
ment is taking necessary steps to ensure that the artistes get the desired benefit. The Committee 
recommends the pro_gressive establishment of a network of organisations to ensure that folk artistes in 
villages are enabled to derive full advantage of the scheme meant for them. Assistance should also be 
given for opening performance centres or auditoria at the village and block level so that artistes could 
perform and interact with each other to improve their particular art forms. 
Multipurpo se cultural complexes at States & National Cultural Complex in Delhi 
46. Under this scheme, financial assistance is proposed to be extended to autonomous bodies for 
settmg up art complexes in the States to improve the quality of life among youth and students and to 
sensitize them to what is aesthetically and morally good in our society and also to expose them to the 
finest forms of creative expressions. 
47. The Committee is not happy with the progress made in the scheme and expresses its serious 
concern over the fact that almost two financial years have elapsed and the projects have not been 
finalised yet. The Committee is also not happy with the idea of creating more and more cultural 
infrastructure in big cities and towns at the cost of rural areas. However, the Committee is satisfied to 
note that multi-purpose complexes, are being set up in smaller towns, rural and backward areas and 
recommends that other schemes being formulated by the Deptt. should also be located in sucn art!aS. 
The Committee also recommends that the National Cultural Complex (Parisar), proposed to be set up 
in Delhi, be established in the trans-Yamuna or outer Delhi areas. 
48. The Committee is also of the view that instead of concentrating only on huge cultural 
complexes, Govt. should set up smaller units where the deprived, under privileged and unprivileged 
may have access to all forms of culture as well as to practice and promote their arts. The Committee 
also holds that the Department may construct multi-purpose stadia in smaller towns and cities which 
could be utilised for sports during the day and for cultural purposes in the evening and night. 
Asia'tic Society, Calcutta 
49. The Asiatic Society, Calcutta, is an institution of national importance involved mainly in 
oriental studies and research, research in humanities and science, publication of periodicals, books 
and other literature. At present, there are around 12 senior fellows and 30 junior research scholars 
attached to the Society. 
50. The Committee is surprised to note that a drastic cut has been resorted to in this year's budget 
allocation for the society. The plan provision has been reduced from Rs. 341.00 lakhs (Revised 
Estimates) during the year 1993-94 to Rs. 200.00 lakhs for the year 1994-95. The provision is 
understood to have been reduced in view of the opening of the Asiatic Society, Bombay. The Committee 
desires that the activities of the Asiatic Society, Calcutta should not suffer pending opening of Asiatic 
Society, Bombay. 

51. No financial assistance has been provided to the Asiatic Society, Bombay, during the Eighth 
Five Year plan. The reason behind this is stated to be that the Planning Commission has earmarked a 
provision of Rs. 200.00 lakhs to be given to the Society as corpus fund. But this fund also has not 
reached the Society so far as it is pending approval from the Ministry of Finance. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that government shotJd expedite the matter and release the amount without 
any further delay. 
Assistance to Cultural Organisations 
52. For promotion and dissemination of Cultur¢ the Department extends financial assistance to 
voluntary organisations under various schemes such as Scheme for Building grants to voluntary 
organisations, Scheme for financial Assistance to Dance, Drama and Theatre Ensembles, Financial 
Assistance for Research Support to voluntary organisations· engaged in Cultural Activities, Grants to 
Institutions I Individuals engaged in literary Activities. 
There' has been only marginal increase in allocations for these schemes and the Committee 
recommends that they should be enhanced adequately. 
Maulana Abul Kalam Azad Centre for Asian Studies 
53. This centre, proposed to be set up in the wake of the centenary celebrations of Maulana Abul 
Kalam Azad, is still not complete. The Committee is surprised to note that this ·year budget provision 
for the Centre has been reduced by Rs. 5 lakhs, for the reasons not acceptable to the Committee. The 
Committee recommends that tLere should be no further delay in the setting up of this Centre. 
Indira Gandhi National Centn: for Arts 
54. The Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts was established in 1985 as an autonomous 
Trust. The Government had contributed to its Corpus Fund Rs. 46.75 crores between 1987-88 and 
1993-94. The balance of Rs. 3.25 crores of the Committed amount has been provided in this year's 
Budget. For the building fund, the Government has so far allocated Rs. 32.35 crores and in this year 
Rs. 16.75 crores have been provided. The Committee regrets to note that even after eight years or 
establishment of the Centre, its main projects including the building are yet to be completed, though 
requisite allocations are being made by the Government. The Committee has been told that work on 
the construction of the building has started in the real sense only in March, 1994. The other activities 
of the Centre like microfilming of unpublished manuscripts and creation and updating of data base are, 
however, in progress. The Committee feels that ~teps should be taken to utilise the funds fully and 
speedily so as to achieve the desired objectives. 
Memorials and Centenaries 
55. The Department of Culture proposes to commemorate this year the 125th birth anniversary of 
Mahatma Gandhi through Gandhi Smriti and Darshan Samiti. But the allocation earmarked for the 
purpose is most inadequate. Also, in 'this year, the country will observe the 75th Anniversary of the 
Jallianwala Bagh Massacre but no budgetary provision has been made for this purpose. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that the budget provision for celebration of the 12Sth birth anniversary of 
Mahatma Gandhi be increased and adequate funds be allocated for the observance of the 7S.th 
Anniversary of Jallianwala Bagh Massacre.

INTRODUCTION

The main objectives of the Department of Health are:-

(i)

(ii)

(iii)

(vi)

to undertake national programmes of health and to intensify measures for the prevention,
control and eradication of communicable diseases;

to promote education, research and training in various medical disciplines, to reorient the
medical colleges in the delivery of health services in rural areas;

to prevent adulteration of food as well as drugs;

to provide primary health care at the doorsteps of the people and to train the required
number of personnel for this purpose;

to take steps for better implementation of Health Care Programmes for tribal and other
weaker sections of the Society; and

to collaborate with member countries of United Nations and International Agencies like
WHO, UNICEF in matters relating to health promotion.

The Department of Health incurs expenditure either directly or through various institutions and
establishments run by it and by way of grants given to autonomous and voluntary organisations. Grants
to States and Union Territory Administrations are mainly for Centrally Sponsored Health Schemes being
implemented through the State Governments and Union Territory Administrations. They include national
programmes for prevention, control and eradication of diseases.

in patient care and/ or research:

IL _ BUDGETARY ALLOCATION

21 A Budgetary provision of Rs. 2354.25 crores has been made for the Department of Health for
2001-2002. Rs. 1432.74 crores is the Plan component and Rs. 921.51 crores have, been provided under
Non-Plan.

2.2 On a specific query as to the projected requirements of the Department under plan 2001-2002,
the Department clarified that a budgetary provision of Rs. 1450.00 crore (including a component of Rs.
17.26 crore under Capital Head) has been made for 2001-2002 against Rs. 1300.00 crores (including a
component of Rs. 22.14 crore under Capital Head) allocated in BE 2000-2001 reduced to Rs. 1159.64
crore in RE 2000-2001. Although the BE for 2001-2002 shows an increase of Rs. 150 crore as compared
to BE for 2000-2001, there is in fact a decline in the approved outlay of Rs. 1450.00 crore for 2001-2002
vis-a-vis the outlay as projected by the Department, 1.९. Rs. 1600.00 crores. It was further clarified that
the requirements originally proposed for Annual Plan 2001-2002 were keeping in view the Ninth Plan
priorities and likely expenditure. Cut of Rs. 150.00 crore in outlay may, therefore, be restored.

2.3 The Committee has observed that allocations (both plan and non-plan) made during Ninth
Plan are invariably being reduced at the RE stage and even this reduced allocation is not fully
utilised. The Committee has been informed that non-finalisation of the procurement agencies as
well as drug supply orders under the National Anti Malaria Programme and National T.B. Control
Programme has resulted in some shortfall in Plan expenditure during initial years of Ninth Plan.
Besides that, time taken in finalisation of modalities for implementation of new projects can also be
held responsible for this trend of expenditure.

24 The Committee is not fully convinced with the justification given by the Department that
there has been increase in percentage of plan expenditure during the Ninth Plan period. During the
Fourth Year of the Ninth Plan, i.e. 2000-2001, Plan allocation of Rs. 1300.00 crores was reduced to
Rs. 1160.00 crores and anticipated expenditure would be Rs. 1120.00 crore. Fact remains that
allocation including both plan and non-plan component continues to be reduced at the RE stage
and even this reduced allocation is not being fully utilised. Tenth Plan is to commence from 2002-
2003. The Committee is of the view that all procedural formalities for ongoing programmes and
new projects to be taken up in Tenth Plan should be completed by the end of the last year of Ninth
Plan, i.e. 2001-2002 so that there is optimum utilization of allocated funds right from the first year
of Tenth Plan.

Ill. CENTRAL GOVERNMENT HEALTH SCHEME(CGHS)

3.1 Rs. 12 crores have been provided under Plan for CGHS for 2001-2002 against an allocation of
Rs. 10 crores in BE 2000-2001 increased to Rs. 10.5 crores at the RE stage. Enhancement in allocation is
proposed to be utilized for provision of new equipments, material and supplies to dispensaries at
Guwahati, Jabalpur and Trivandrum, subject to usual clearances. The Committee finds that during 2000-
2001, utilization position upto 31.12.2000 has not been very encouraging. (Against a plan provision of


Rs. 12.50 crore, both under revenue and capital head, expenditure is only Rs. 4.76 crore). The
Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts should be initiated in right earnest for obtaining
usual clearances so that funds are utilised to the optimum during 2001-2002.

3.2 During the Ninth Plan. CGHS facilities were to be extended to the cities of Chandigarh, Bhopal
and Shillong alongwith addition of four new Allopathic dispensaries. However, all exercise has been held
up due to the time taken in completion of the procedural formalities/action as given in the SIU Report of
November, 1999 on the Norms study of the CGHS (Allopathic) dispensaries. The Committee notes that
the Department has finally accepted the SIU Report and conveyed its decision to DG (Health Services) on
16" February, 2001. EFC note is to be prepared now. The Committee apprehends that exercise of
creation of additional new posts under CGHS would not be complete during 2001-2002 also which
is the last year of Ninth Plan. The Committee, therefore, strongly, recommends that the
Department should make serious efforts to expedite the creation of posts, essential for expansion of
CGHS network.

3.3 The Department has informed that an Inspection Team has been constitutated for making
surprise visits to various CGHS dispensaries. Sixty surprise checks from September, 2000 to February
2001 have been carried out in Delhi. Five checks were carried out in Kolkata. The Committee finds that
as a result of these inspections, steps have been taken to expedite the supply of medicines etc. The
Committee is, however, of the view that inspection teams should also inter-act with patients visiting
the dispensary to have an idea about the problems being faced by them.

3.4 Last year, the Committee was informed that the Reports of Das Gupta and Roy Choudhary
Committees on formulation of a single comprehensive drug formulary for CGHS and MSO were
reviewed by a Committee under the Chairmanship of DGHS and a fresh Committee was under the
consideration of the Department. The Committee notes that a new Committee under the Chairmanship of
Prof. J.N. Pande of AIIMS has been constituted on 16" November, 2000 which is expected to submit its
report by 30" April, 2001 The Committee feels that the exercise for formulating a single
comprehensive formulary for CGHS and MSO has been dragging on for a very long period. The
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Department should ensure that the latest
committee completes the task assigned to it within the scheduled time limit so that a single
comprehensive drug formulary for CGHS and MSO is brought out without any further delay.

IV. SAFDARJUNG HOSPITAL

41 The Plan allocation for Safdarjung Hospital for the year 2001-2002 is Rs. 22.00 crores. The
Department has informed that the projected demand for Safdarjung Hospital for 2001-2002 was Rs. 29.93
crores.

4.2. The Committee notes that Plan allocation of Rs. 28.00 crores for Safdarjung Hospital in 2000-
2001 was reduced to Rs. 26.00 crores at the RE stage. The Department has informed that this reduction
was due to the saving in the Salary Head (Plan) due to non-fulfilment of vacant posts during the year.
Besides that, the Central Monitoring Station with monitors for Burns and Plastic Ward costing nearly Rs.
1.20 crores could not be purchased during 2000-2001 as the specifications of requirements were being re-
checked. The Committee observes that the Central Monitoring Station could not be procured during 1999-
2000 due to hike in its price. Procurement of another equipment of Cath. Lab was also held up due to
alleged irregularities.

43 The Committee expresses its serious concern on the declining trend in the utilization of Plan
allocation for Safdarjung Hospital as indicated below:-

4.4 Last year, while commenting on unsatisfactory services being provided by Safdarjung
Hospital, the Committee had observed that the Department should find out ways and means of
maintaining cleanliness in all Govt. Hospitals. The Department has informed that the Employees
Unions have strongly objected to entrusting the work for doing peripheral jobs to private parties.
The Committee strongly feels that the Department is failing in its duty of providing required
services to public by taking shelter behind the stand taken by Employees Unions. The Committee is
of the view that in such a scenario, the Department should resort to strict measures so that
employees are made to carry out the duties assigned to them.

Vv. DR. RAM MANOHAR LOHBIA HOSPITAL

5.1 Plan allocation for the Dr. RML hospital, New Delhi has been substantially decreased from Rs.
24.50 crores in 2000-2001 to Rs. 20.00 crores at RE stage. On a specific query as to the reason for
decrease, the Department has replied that the decrease was due to the slow place of expenditure shown by
the Hospital. The Hospital has incurred an expenditure of only Rs. 4.88 crores till October, 2000 and
expenditure figures upto 13.3.2001 are Rs. 14.40 crores. Plan allocation for the Hospital for 2001-2002
is Rs. 21.00 crores. The Committee is of the view that serious efforts need to be made for optimum
utilization of allocated funds within the targetted period.

5.2. The Committee has been commenting on the issue of building up a Trauma Centre at Dr. R.M.L.
Hospital for the last two three years. Last year, the Committee was informed that the work of Trauma
Centre had been entrusted to the Hospital Services Consultancy Corporation and a draft EFC proposal
was likely to be submitted shortly. The progress made during 2000-2001 is that the draft EFC paper has
been submitted by HSCC and is in the process of approval by DGHS/Ministry. In this process, a
memoranduim has been prepared and circulated to the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance
whose comments have since been received. The clarification/reply on the comments of the Planning
Commission and Ministry of Finance are being prepared now. The Department has informed that the
time schedule for completion of the project can be indicated only after the approval of EFC. The
Committee is perturbed to observe that although considerable time has passed, the construction
work on the project of a Trauma Centre at Dr. R.M.L. Hospital is yet to start. A number of


formalities still remain to be completed. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the approval
of EFC on the project should be expedited so that construction work on Trauma Centre can start
without any further delay.

VI. CENTRAL INSTITUTE OF PSYCHIATRY, RANCHI

6.1 The Plan allocation for the Institute in BE 2000-2001 was Rs. 3.00 crores, which has been
substantially increased to Rs. 7.00 crores in BE 2001-2002. The Department has informed that the
reason for additional allocation of funds to the tune of Rs. 4 crores is that CIP, Ranchi proposes to
Procure a number of major machines and equipments i.e. Spiral CT Scan, Colour Doppler, Computer
Server, EEG machine and accessories and Biochemistry and Haemotological Anaalyzer. The Committee
hopes that concerted efforts would be made by CIP, Ranchi so that the exercise of purchasing the
proposed machines and equipments is completed during 2001-2002 thereby avoiding reduction of
allocation at the RE stage.

6.2 The Committee notes that the issue of creation of 260 posts as recommended by IWSU study
conducted for CIP, Ranchi submitted on 16.01.97 is under fresh examination. The Committee finds that
in the meantime a team from the National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro-Surgery (NIMHANS)
sent to CIP, Ranchi on 19 -20" May, 2000 has submitted its detailed recommendations regarding
improvements in infrastructure and staffing on 47 July, 2000. The latest position is that a fresh proposal
which will include recreation of certain posts as well as restructuring of the Staffing Patter is under
preparation.

6.3. IWSU study conducted for CIP, Ranchi had recommended creation of 260 posts as early as
on 16.1.97. The Committee is not able to understand the rationale for having another study
conducted by NIMHANS in May, 2000. The Committee apprehends that this new exercise may lead
to further delay due to a number of procedural formalities which will be started afresh now. The
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Department should make concerted efforts to
expedite the process of modernization of CIP, Ranchi.

VIL - ALL INDIA INSTITUTE OF MEDICAL SCIENCES (AIMS)

TA ‘The All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi is a premier medical institution of the
country.; The Plan allocation for the Institute in BE 2000-2001 was Rs. 91.30 crores, which was reduced
to Rs. 85 crores in RE. On being asked about the reasons for reduction in RE, the Department stated that
this was due to overall resource crunch faced by the Ministry of Health. Plan allocation for 2001-2002
is Rs. 100.00 crores. The Committee notes that the enhanced provision is meant for the creation of
additional wards, labs and ICUs at the Cardiothoracic and Neurosciences Centre, for equipping the organ
retrieval bank, for setting up the Positron Emission Tomography facility and for starting work on the
Apex Trauma Care Centre. The Committee hopes that all the proposed plans and projects would be

XL NATIONAL LEPROSY ERADICATION PROGRAMME

11.1. The objective of the National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP) was to achieve
elimination of leprosy by the year 2000 A.D. by reducing the case load to less than 1/10,000 population.
The Programme received further boost in 1993-94 with sanction of World Bank assistance of Rs.302
crores for a period of 6 years. Phase I of World Bank Project was completed on 30 September, 2000.

11.2. The Committee has been informed that only 20% of leprosy patients are of infectious type and
with modem Multi Drug Therapy, the patient becomes non-infectious very rapidly. Multi Drug Therapy is
being implemented through District Leprosy Societies. The Department has informed that the World
Bank funded programme which is in its fifth year has reduced the prevalence rate from 24/10000 in 1992
to 4.1/10000 in December, 2000. To give continued thrust to 5 highly endemic States of Bihar, U.P.,
M_P., Orissa and West Bengal and also maintenance of gains in other States, the proposal for 2™ Phase of
World Bank assistance for 3 years is being prepared which is targetted for achieving elimination of
leprosy by the end of year 2003 and for completing the process of integration of leprosy services with
General Health Care.

11.3. Two rounds of Modified Leprosy Elimination Campaign a major initiative under the programme
have been implemented so far. During the first MLEC held in 1998-99, 4.64 lakhs cases and during 2™
MLEC held in 1999-2000, 2.12 lakh new cases were detected. The Committee notes with appreciation
that the Modified Leprosy Elimination Campaigns have provided the pace of acceleration for
achieving elimination by detecting and treating large number of cases even in areas where Multi
Drug Therapy (MDT) services were well implemented in last 15 years. The Committee also
expresses its satisfaction with various measures being taken for medical rehabilitation of leprosy-
cured persons.

XII NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR CONTROL OF BLINDNESS

12.1 The aim of the National Programme for Control of Blindness launched in 1976 is to reduce the
blindness rate from 1.49% to 0.3% by 2000 A.D. The budget for various service components under this
Programme has been enhanced since 1994-95 after the launching of World Bank Assisted Cataract
Blindness Control Project. Besides that, Danish and WHO assistance is also being provided for
prevention of blindness. Expenditure position has been quite satisfactory. Performance of Cataract
Operations has been steadily increasing from 16 lakhs in 1992-93 to 35 lakhs in 1999-2000. It has been
informed that the States of Gujarat, Punjab, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Delhi and UTs of
Pondicherry and Chandigarh have attained the Cataract surgery rate of 400 operations per lakh population
required for clearing the backlog of cataract blindness. However, the Committee is constrained to note
that Bihar, Assam and Orissa are among the lowest performing Sta:es having cataract surgery rate
of <200/lakh. A number of Assessment/Facility Surverys have been conducted since 1997 in a large
number of districts in the country. One of the main findings of these surveys is that cataract was still the
leading cause of blindness in 55% of blind persons. In view of the above, the Committee feels that the
Department should closely monitor the implementation of all components of National Programme
for Control of Blindness in all the bad performing States, specially Bihar, Assam and Orissa.


12.2 The Committee notes that 13 districts have been selected in Phase I of the National Survey
on Blindness, results of which are likely to be available by the end of year 2001. The Committee
feels that results when received would help in better implementation of the Programme.

12.3. The Committee is of the view that concerted efforts are required to be made for enhancing
the coverage of eye care services in tribal and other under-served areas. The Committee,
therefore, feels that this exercise should be taken up at the earliest in a time bound Action Plan.

XII NATIONAL AIDS CONTROL PROGRAMME

13.1 The Plan allocation for the Programme has been increased from Rs.145.00 crores in BE 2000-
2001 to Rs.180.00 crores in RE 2000-2001. Apart from this, a separate provision of Rs.30 crores has been
kept for the N.E States.

13.2 The Committee is perturbed to note that HIV/AIDS infection has percolated into general
population during the past few years and presently no state remains unaffected. The National AIDS
Control Programme phase II has been launched from 9" November 1999 with the two key objectives
namely to reduce the spread of HIV infection in India and strengthen India’s capacity to respond to the
HIV/AIDS on a long term basis. There has been optimum utilisation of funds allocated for NACP -
against an allocation of Rs.140.00 crores in 1999-2000 - utilisation was Rs.135.27 crores. Similarly, an
expenditure of Rs. 168.69 crores has been incurred upto 13.3.2001 out of Rs.180.00 crores provided in
2000-2001

13.3. The Committee apprehends that very high cost of treatment of HIV/AIDS infection would
be further affected with the advent of new patent regime from 2005. The Committee takes note of
the Department’s stand that the provision for a compulsory licensing for manufacturing of drugs
for public non-commercial use should be secured. The Department is also trying to impress WHO
to use international funding for purchasing patents so that major vaccines and therapeutic drugs
including AIDS come within the public domain.

13.4... At present, 563 NGOs are being funded under the Programme. The Committee observes that
NGOs are being involved as critical partners in the following important thrust areas :-

- Targetted interventions for the high risk and marginalized population;
- School AIDS Education;

- Low cost community care for people living with HIV/AIDS;

- Counselling; and

- Family Health Awareness Campaigns.

Selection of specific NGOs and the release of funds is now being done by the State AIDS Control
Societies. The Committee has been given to understand that the release of central funds directly to State
AIDS Control Societies, instead of chanelising the funds through State Governments has resulted in better
utilisation of funds.

13.5 The Committee has, however, a word of caution. At present, what is a happening is that
that NGOs are concentrated in metropolitan cities and also where State AIDS Control Societies are
functioning well. The Committee strongly feels that the Department should conduct a survey so as
to assess which are the districts where NGO activity is simply not there and take up the matter with
the State Society for attracting NGOs towards this social activity.

13.6 The Committee is of the view that inspite of there being a fool proof procedure for selection
of NGOs under NACP, ground realities in some areas are entirely different. Regular and intensive


monitoring of NGOs is very essential for checking undesirable activities. Stringent measures need
to be taken against blacklisted NGOs. The Committee feels that besides NGOs, the Department
should also explore the possibility of involving some other agency in this area.

13.7... It has come to the notice of the Committee that research being done by Indian Scientists in
this critical area is not receiving the desired support from the Central Government. AIDS kits
developed by some Bangalore Scientists although approved by WHO did not receive recognition of
the Government. The Committee has a feeling that vested interests are coming in the way of
indigenous attempts. Government should provide all possible support, if some genuine research is
there.

XIV NATIONAL TB CONTROL PROGRAMME

14.1 India accounts for nearly one third of Global TB burden and every year has more than 2 million
new cases of TB. Based on the past experience, a Revised Strategy for National TB Control Programme
was evolved by the Government with the aim to achieve a cure rate of over 85% and augmentation of
case finding activities to detect at least 70% estimated cases. This strategy was pilot-tested with SIDA
assistance in 1993-94 on a population of 2.35 million. Since then, in a phased manner till January, 2001 a
population of about 330 million has been covered. With support of DFID and DANIDA, the population
coverage under RNTCP will be increased to about 500 million by 2002. Phase II of the Programme is
under preparation for funding under World Bank for further expansion upto 700 million population.

good. Detection rate has been 120/10,000 against a target of 135/10,000. The average cure rate has
been 80% against the target of 85%. The Committee notes that due to Government machinery not
being available to the public in many areas, the Department is exploring the possibility of
implementing the programme through private practitioners. A pilot study on distribution of drugs
through private practitioners is being conducted in East Delhi. The Committee is of the view that
the Department should take all precautions before taking such an initiative.

XVII HOSPITAL WASTE MANAGEMENT

17.1 Hospital Waste is one of the biggest health hazards that is being faced by every citizen of this
country. The Committee has been informed that 21 State Governments/Union Territories have constituted
Advisory Committees for implementation of Bio-Medical Waste (Management and Handling) Rules,
1998. The extended deadline dated 30.6.2000 to initiate treatment and disposal of bio-medical wastes for
towns with a population of 30 lakhs and above and others having hospitals with 500 beds and more has
already ended. The Committee views with serious concern that the implementation status by the
States/UTs are yet to be received by the Central Pollution Control Board.

17.2. The Committee apprehends that there are very little chances of any progress being made
and conditions of hospitals/nursing homes would continue to be health hazardous. The Central
Government cannot take shelter behind the plea that health is a state subject. Need of the hour is
that Central Government should initiate some effective steps by entering into a meaningful
dialogue with State Governments.

XVII QUALITY CONTROL OF DRUGS

Quality Control of Drugs continues to be a weak area. The Committee observes that there is a
need of taking effective steps both at the Centre and State level for strengthening the Central and State
Drugs Control Organisations. It has been informed that funds are being provided by the Centre for
purchase of equipments by State Drug Testing Labs. Similarly, additional testing equipments are also
being provided to the Central Drug Labs. The Committee is of the view that the Department should
vigorously pursue the maximum utilization of allocated funds by State Governments and prevail upon the
State Govts to strengthen the State structures by providing funds to the extent possible. The Committee
finds that Delhi, Gujarat, Maharashtra, MP, Karnataka and West Bengal are having the maximum
number of vacant posts of Drug Inspectors. The Department should take up the matter with the
concerned State Governments. The Committee is of the view that the proposed establishment of
two new Central Labs at Chandigarh and Hyderabad should be taken up on a priority basis
without any further delay.

XIX NATIONAL ILLNESS ASSISTANCE FUND

The Committee notes that there have been savings in the allocation made under National 11655
Assistance Fund due to non-setting up of the funds by State Governments. and non-receipt of proposals
by State Governments. And also due to lesser release of central assistance than anticipated owing to the
fact that States earlier sanctioned grants-in-aid have not submitted utilization certificates. Grant-in-aid to
State Governments is limited to 50% of the State contribution. Although 15 States have set up Illness
Assistance Fund, lack of resources is one of the reasons for States not contributing to this head. Besides
that, lack of publicity can also be held to be responsible for non-utilisation of funds. The Committee
feels that the Department should make concerted efforts by pursuing with State Governments to
actively implement the scheme of National Illness Assistance Fund. The Committee feels that,
public at large is not aware about the scheme. Efforts should therefore be made both at State and
Central level to give wide publicity to the scheme so that this fund could be fully utilised for the
purpose for which it has been set up.

20.1 Regarding amendment of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 and approaching a larger Bench of

the Supreme Court so that service rendered by doctors of Government Hospitals/CGHS dispensaries
come within its purview, the Department has replied that such a step would require wide ranging

20.2 The Committee expresses its strong reservation on the evasive stand being taken by the

their part. On the other hand, Government doctors, by being not covered under the Consumer
Protection Act, continue to enjoy a comfortable position at the cost of patients coming under their
treatment. This kind of discriminatory position leads to serious complications in some cases. The
Committee is not convinced with the argument that standards at Government Hospitals being very
low, doctors posted there cannot no be held responsible for their lapses. The Committee, therefore,
reiterates is its earlier recommendation to make necessary amendment in the relevant Section of
the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 so as to bring Govt. Doctors within its purview.

20.3 The Committee notes that at present Members of Parliament get reimbursement in respect
of treatment taken in a private recognized hospital as per the package rates prescribed by the

treatment in private medical institutions for sitting M.Ps. and have now been given to Lok Sabha

JIPMER. The Committee strongly recommends that situation of vacant posts and non-creation of
required posts should not be allowed to be continued for long in a teaching Institute. The
Department should initiate necessary steps in this direction and get allocated required funds for the
purpose. (Para 5.2)

NATIONAL CANCER RESEARCH PROGRAMME

The Committee has been informed that evaluation of the programme has been entrusted to
the National Institute of Health and Family Welfare on 22" November, 2000. The Committee
hopes that findings of this evaluation would lead to strengthening of the National Cancer Research
Programme. (Para 9.2)

While appreciating the various measures being taken under the National Cancer Research
Programme, the Committee observes that in quite a few states, Regional Cancer Centres have not
been established so far. NE States of Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland,
Manipur, Tripura and Sikkim are not having a RCC at present. The Committee feels that there is
a need for establishing one Regional Cancer Centre in NE Region and recommends that action
may be initiated in this direction. (Para 9.4)

NATIONAL MALARIA ERADICATION PROGRAMME

The Committee is constrained to note that instead of there being any improvement in
achieyement level in 1999-2000, it has declined - against a target of 171.40 million population
targetted, coverage level is only 60.66 million. (Para 10.3)

The Committee has observed that these constraints are being faced for a number of years.
The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Department should vigorously pursue this

17


aspect with the concerned State Governments so as to improve the achievement level of various
physical targets of NMEP. (Para 10.4)

The Committee is, however, constrained to note that instead of furnishing the information
asked for, procedure for release of funds to District Malaria Control Societies has been explained.
The Committee would like to be apprised about the utilization position of funds by State
Governments covered under EMCP. (Para 10.5)

NATIONAL LEPROSY ERADICATION PROGRAMME

The Committee notes with appreciation that the Modified Leprosy Elimination Campaigns
have provided the pace of acceleration for achieving elimination by detecting and treating large
number of cases even in areas where Multi Drug Therapy (MDT) services were well implemented
in last 15 years. The Committee also expresses its satisfaction with various measures being taken
for medical rehabilitation of leprosy-cured persons. (Para 11.3)

NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR CONTROL OF BLINDNESS

However, the Committee is constrained to note that Bihar, Assam and Orissa are among the
lowest performing States having cataract surgery rate of <200/lakh. In view of the above, the
Committee feels that the Department should closely monitor the implementation of all components
of National Programme for Control of Blindness in all the bad performing States, specially Bihar,
Assam and Orissa. (Para 12.2)

The Committee notes that 13 districts have been selected in Phase I of the National Survey
on Blindness, results of which are likely to be available by the end of year 2001. The Committee
feels that results when received would help in better implementation of the Programme. (Para 12.2)

The Committee is of the view that concerted efforts are required to be made for enhancing
the coverage of eye care services in tribal and other under-served areas. The Committee,
therefore, feels that this exercise should be taken up at the earliest in a time bound Action Plan.
(Para 12.3)

NATIONAL AIDS CONTROL PROGRAMME

The Committee apprehends that very high cost of treatment of HIV/AIDS infection would
be further affected with the advent of new patent regime from 2005. The Committee takes note of
the Department’s stand that the provision for a compulsory licensing for manufacturing of drugs
for public non-commercial use should be secured. The Department is also trying to impress WHO
to use international funding for purchasing patents so that major vaccines arid therapeutic drugs
including AIDS come within the public domain. (Para 13.3)

The Committee has, however, a word of caution. At present, what is a happening is that
that NGOs are concentrated in metropolitan cities and also where State AIDS Control Societies are
functioning well. The Committee strongly feels that the Department should conduct a survey so as
to assess which are the districts where NGO activity is simply not there and take up the matter with
the State Society for attracting NGOs towards this social activity. (Para 13.5)

The Committee is of the view that inspite of there being a fool proof procedure for selection

of NGOs under NACP, ground realities in some areas are entirely different. Regular and intensive
monitoring of NGOs is very essential for checking undesirable activities. Stringent measures need

18


to be taken against blacklisted NGOs. The Committee feels that besides NGOs, the Department
should also explore the possibility of involving some other agency in this area. (Para 13.6)

It has come to the notice of the Conunittee that research being done by Indian Scientists in
this critical area is not receiving the desired support from the Central Government. AIDS kits
developed by some Bangalore Scientists although approved by WHO did not receive recognition of
the Government. The Committee has a feeting that vested interests are coming in the way of
indigenous attempts. Government should provide all possible support, if some genuine research is
there. (Para 13.7)

NATIONAL TB CONTROL PROGRAMME

The Committee has been informed that achievements under the Programme have been very
good. Detection rate has been 120/10,000 against a target of 13$/10,000. The average cure rate has
been 80% against the target of 85%. The Committee notes that due to Government machinery not
being available to the public in many areas, the Department is exploring the possibility of
implementing the programme through private practitioners. A pilot study on distribution of drugs
through private practitioners is being conducted in East Delhi. The Committee is of the view that
the Department should take all precautions before taking such an initiative. (Para 14.2)

The Committee fails to understand that inspite of such an impressive set up, both physical and
financial targets continue to show under achievement level. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that beside analysing reports at the centre and holding of meetings with project state officials,
random surveys/surprise inspections by Central teams are also very much required. The
Committee is of the view that interaction with local public representatives to the extent possible
may result in bringing out ground realities. Department should explore the possibility in this
direction and evolve a more effective monitoring mechanism. (Para 14.6)

STATE HEALTH SYSTEMS DEVELOPMENT PROJECTS

While welcoming this initiative, the Committee would like to be apprised about the findings
of assessment of project undertaken in Andhra Pradesh which was launched on 11 March, 1995 for
a period of 6 % years. (Para 15.2)

IMPLEMENTATION OF HEALTH PROGRAMMES IN NORTH EAST SECTOR

16.2. The Committee is of the view that the Department should closely monitor the utilization of
funds under the various health programmes in NE region. Department should also take effective
steps for removing the constraints being faced by NE states which can lead to proper
implementation of all the health programmes being carried out there. (Para 16.2)

HOSPITAL WASTE MANAGEMENT

The Committee views with serious concern that the implementation status by the
States/UTs are yet to be received by the Central Pollution Control Board. (Para 17.1)

The Committee apprehends that there are very little chances of any progress being made
and conditions of hospitals/nursing homes would continue to be health hazardous. The Central
Government cannot take shelter behind the plea that health is a state subject. Need of the hour is
that Central Government should initiate some effective steps by entering into a meaningful dialogue
with State Governments. (Para 17.2)


QUALITY CONTROL OF DRUGS

The Committee finds that Delhi, Gujarat, Maharashtra, MP, Karnataka and West Bengal
are having the maximum number of vacant posts of Drug Inspectors. The Department should take
up the matter with the concerned State Governments. The Committee is of the view that the
proposed establishment of two new Central Labs at Chandigarh and Hyderabad should be taken
up on a priority basis without any further delay. (Para 18)

NATIONAL ILLNESS ASSISTANCE FUND

The Committee feels that the Department should make concerted efforts by pursuing with
State Governments to actively implement the scheme of National Illness Assistance Fund. The
Committee feels that public at large is not aware about the scheme. Efforts should therefore be
made both at State and Central level to give wide publicity to the scheme so that this fund could be
fully utilised for the purpose for which it has been set up. (Para 19)

GENERAL

20.2. The Committee expresses its strong reservation on the evasive stand being taken by the
Department on such a vital issue Private doctors can be taken to court for any act of negligence on
their part. On the other hand, Government doctors, by being not covered under the Consumer
Protection Act, continue to enjoy a comfortable position at the cost of patients coming under their
treatment. This kind of discriminatory position leads to serious complications in some cases. The
Committee is not convinced with the argument that standards at Government Hospitals being very
low, doctors posted there cannot no be held responsible for their lapses. The Committee, therefore,
reiterates is its earlier recommendation to make necessary amendment in the relevant Section of
the ConsumerProtection Act, 1986 so as to bring Govt. Doctors within its purview. (Para 20.2)

The Committee notes that at present Members of Parliament get reimbursement in respect
of treatment taken in a private recognized hospital as per the package rates prescribed by the
CGHS. The Secretary clarified that full powers of passing bills for reimbursement of medical
treatment in private medical institutions for sitting M.Ps. and have now been given to Lok Sabha
/Rajya Sabha Secretariats. The Committee finds this misleading. (20.3)

REPORT
I.          INTRODUCTION
1.1       India with just 2.4% of the world landmass constitutes 16% of the present world population.  The census of 1991
had indicated the population of India as 846.3 million.  In the decade of 1981-91, 163 million persons were added to the
population of India.  On 11 th May, 2000, the population of India has already crossed 1 billion mark.   If the present rate
of annual growth of population  of 1.74% continues, India may overtake China in 2045 to become the most populous
country in the world.
1.2      With a view to check  the growth of population, the Family Welfare Programme was taken up with the
introduction of Planning in the country.  The objective of the Family Welfare Programme for the country has been to
stabilise population at a level consistent with the needs of national development.  To achieve this goal the Department
continues to implement the three-pronged strategy of :
(i)         improvement in the health status of women and children;
(ii)        fulfillment of the unmet needs of contraception with a special focus on widening the range of choice
available to the people; and
(iii)       professionalising and broad-basing the Information, Education     and Communication Campaign (IEC)
on Family Welfare, by not only using the mass media, but also involving the community, NGOs,
women’s organisations in the local specific IEC work at the district, sub-district and village level.
1.3       The latest achievements of the National Family Welfare Programme as furnished by the Department, are

1.6.      The Committee notes that though there is a continuous decline in various demographic indicators over the years,
they are still very high in comparison to other developing countries like Sri Lanka, Indonesia, China and Cuba.  The
Committee, therefore, feels that rural and inaccessible areas are still outside the reach of Family Welfare Programme 
and unless these  areas are covered by the various Family Welfare Programmes, there cannot be any significant decline
in the abovementioned indicators and the growth of population will remain unabated.
II.         BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       The Committee notes that the allocation for the Department has been reduced from Rs. 3541.47 crores in  BE
2000-2001 to Rs. 3221.37 crores at the RE stage.  However, a provision of Rs. 4232.28 crores has been made in BE
2001-2002 which represents an increase of Rs. 690.81 crores over the previous year.  
2.2       Commenting on the allocation made to the Department, it has been stated that in the Annual Plan proposal for
the year 2001-2002 sent to the Planning Commission, a requirement of Rs. 5922.72 crores was projected.   However, an
allocation of only Rs. 4210 crores  for 2001-2002 has been made by the Planning Commission.  As a result of the cut in
the Plan proposal, there is likely to be an accumulation of arrears and inadequate funding on infrastructure side of
various programmes and activities like RCH Programme, contraceptive supplies and maintenance of expenditure on
Rural Family Welfare Centres, etc.  
2.3       The Department has further informed that in the case of Rural Family Welfare Centres  the outlay proposed by it
was Rs. 700.00 crores and the outlay approved was Rs. 430.00 crores.  In the case of Sub-Centres the outlay proposed
was Rs. 1237.00 crores and the outlay approved was Rs. 675.00 crores.  In the case of maintenance of Urban Family
Welfare Centres, outlay proposed was Rs. 53.33 crores and the outlay approved was Rs. 35.00 crores. 
2.4       The Committee notes that the Eleventh Finance Commission agreed with the views of the Committee that the
transfer of cost of maintenance of infrastructure under Family Welfare Programme to the States would impose
enormous liability on them and weaken their resources and also there is no guarantee that the transferred funds would be
used for Family Welfare Programme.   The Committee, therefore, reiterates  its earlier recommendation that status quo
in this regard should be maintained.
III.       RURAL FAMILY WELFARE SERVICES
3.1       An enhanced allocation of Rs. 1105.00 crores has been made for Rural Family Welfare Services when compared
to BE provision of Rs. 921.00 crore in 2000-2001. The break-up of  total allocation for Rural Family Welfare Services is

3.2       There are at present 5435 Rural Family Welfare Centres functioning in the country which were established at all
the block level PHCs sanctioned upto 1.4.80.  These centres are entrusted with the responsibility for implementing the
Family Welfare Programme, i.e. planning, mobilisation, monitoring, administration and supervision in their areas.  
Block level PHCs have either replaced a PHC or got strengthened as CHC.   Besides that, to provide basic health and
family welfare services to the rural population, 1,37,271 Sub-centres are currently functioning, out of which 97,757 Sub
centres are funded by Govt. of India and the rest are funded under the State Minimum Needs/Basic Minimum Services
Programme.
3.3       Sub-Centres and PHCs provide basic health and family welfare services  and implement the Family Welfare
Programme in all respects.  The Committee observes that all India achievement level of targets set for 1999-2000 by the
Planning Commission in respect of Sub-Centres /PHCs / CHCs is as follows :-

3.4.      The Committee is constrained to note that the Sub-Centres,  PHCs and CHCs set up during 1999-2000 are
pathetically below the set target.   A few States/UT like Bihar, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, U.P., West Bengal
and Delhi have done nothing to open Sub-Centres, PHCs, CHCs, in 1999-2000.
3.5.      The Committee was given to understand that there was a proposal from the Finance Ministry last year that if any
Panchayati Raj Institution was willing to contribute up to 20% of the required funds for establishing a new sub-centre in
their area, the Centre and State will equally share  the remaining cost of establishing a new sub centre.  Thus, the cost
will be shared by the Centre, State & PRI in the ratio of 40:40:20.  The State Government will be responsible for
bearing the recurring cost of the sub-centres thus created . However, there has been no consensus among the States in
favour of this scheme due to their tight financial position.  Therefore, Department of Family Welfare has requested the
Ministry of Finance to consider financing the scheme as a 100% Centrally Sponsored Scheme. The Committee
recommends that Ministry of Finance should consider the proposal of the Department of Family Welfare in view of
meagre financial resources of most of the States.
3.6.      The Committee understands that during 9th Plan, highest priority has been given to bridge the gap between the
number of primary health care institutions  required to cover the 1991 population as per the existing norms for
population coverage and those actually functioning.  Following targets for the establishment of Sub-Centres, PHCs and

These targets were set as per 1991 population.   The present requirement would be much more in view of the high rate
of population growth.     The Committee therefore, urges upon the Department to take necessary steps so that in future
the targets for setting up of Sub-centres, PHCs, CHCs are achieved particularly in case of weak performing States/UTs.
The Committee, at the same time, emphasizes that the targets fixed need to be realistic taking into consideration the
financial constraints of all the States/UTs.
3.7.      The Committee was informed that a Consultative Committee was set up by the Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare on the recommendation of the Planning Commission to examine the revision of Schemes on maintenance of
infrastructure and manpower.  Among other recommendations, one pertained to the proposal of Government of India
accepting the responsibility of funding all the existing sub-centres in exchange for the States accepting the financial
liability for supporting the Rural Family Welfare  Centres.  It was observed that out of the existing 1,37,271 sub-centres,
only 97,757 were being funded by the Central Government and the rest were being funded by the respective State
Govts. from their own resources. The Consultative Committee reasoned that the additional liability of the Central
Government in accepting the recurring expenditure of the remaining Sub-Centres would be Rs. 421 crore whereas it was
already spending Rs. 439 crore in maintenance of the RFWCs. Therefore, the Consultative Committee  recommended a
swap of these responsibilities between the Central Government and  the States.  The Committee feels that the issue 
needs to be discussed with the State Governments/UT Administrations before any decision is taken in this regard for

V.           REPRODUCTIVE AND CHILD HEALTH  PROGRAMME (RCH)
5.1.         The concept of RCH Programme is to provide need-based, client-oriented, demand-driven, high quality and
integrated RCH services to the beneficiaries. The RCH programme is a composite programme incorporating the inputs
of the Government of India as well as funding support from external donor agencies including the  World Bank and the
European Commission. 
5.2.         The Programme aims at meeting the unmet needs of Family Welfare Programme by improving health status of
women and children, especially the poor and underserved, by reducing infant, child and maternal mortality and
morbidity through:-
 
(a)
          Sustaining and strengthening the ongoing Child Survival and Safe Motherhood Programme to ensure the
essential services as per package of services;
(b)         Improving the performance of the Family Welfare System in implementing policy change;
(c)          Strengthening  the quality and effectiveness of the services under essential package of Reproductive and
Child Health Services;
(d)         Improving project implementation through the application of performance based criteria for continued
funding; and
(e)          implementing and managing project activities by following certain fixed benchmarks.
5.3.         Allocation of Rs.951.00 crores was made in BE 2000-2001 which was reduced to Rs.801.00 crores at the RE
stage. Allocation in BE 2001-2002 has been substantially enhanced to Rs.1126.95 crores. On being asked as to how the
additional allocation will be utilized, the Department informed that the additional allocation is because of release of
funds direct to SCOVA Committees formed in the States to avoid delay while routing funds through the State Finance
Departments. The increase is proposed to be utilized in the following components.
(A)
        RCH Other interventions-

category C districts.
(ii)                Dais Training
(iii)               Out-reach Services – Presently being implemented in 50 districts, proposed to be extended to
another 100 districts covering thereby 150 districts in all.
(iv)              Hepatitis-B Project – A new Pilot Project on Hepatitis B at a cost of Rs.9.27 crores proposed to
be taken up during 2001-2002.
(v)                Financial Envelope – Currently, provided to 4 States only, proposed to extend it to 2 more
States during the next year.

XI        DISTRIBUTION OF CONTRACEPTIVES
11.1.    An allocation of Rs. 108.71 crores was made under the head ‘Free Distribution of Conventional Contraceptives’
in BE in 2000-01 which was reduced to Rs. 95.71 crores at the RE stage.  However, allocation in BE 2001-2002 has
been increased to Rs. 117.00 crores.  Explaining the reasons for this variation, the Department has informed that
reduction at RE 2000-2001 was mainly due to unexpected less expenditure in the procurement of Copper T, less
procurement of  Mala N on account of less demand from the States, and limited number of Laparoscopes procured. 
However, allocation in BE 2001-2002 has been increased mainly due to more demand of free supply of Nirodh from the
State Governments. The increase in allocation in 2001-2002 is also due to the fact that cost of raw material has been
added in the proposed BE as UNFPA  has discontinued the supply of  raw material as commodity assistance for
manufacturing  of Oral Contraceptive pills.
11.2.   The Committee has been informed that according to the studies conducted by the International Institute of
Population Studies, Mumbai in Haryana, Maharashtra and UP revealed that around sixty percent of condoms under free
distribution system was unused and wasted.  Hence, in order to minimize wastage and promote distribution of
comdoms, a scheme of service charge of ten paise per condom, to be retained by the health worker, was introduced
during 1997-98.  However, subsequent survey revealed that this new incentive did not reach most of the doctors and
health workers in PHC/ Sub Centres.
11.3.    The Committee feels that the scheme of service charge of ten paise per condom to be retained by the health
worker is  good except for the fact that ten paise per condom is too meagre an amount to attract the enthusiasm of the
health workers.  The Committee is also disturbed to know that this new scheme did not reach most of the doctors and
health workers in the sub centres.  This means that the funds  earmarked for the purpose are being squandered by the
middlemen instead of reaching the health workers.  The Committee views this as a serious lapse in monitoring the
utilization of funds by the Department and recommends that  corrective measures may be taken in this regard.

XIII.        NATIONAL POPULATION POLICY
13.1.       The Committee notes that after many years of deliberation and consultation, the National Population Policy,
was presented to Parliament last year.  The Committee has been informed that the immediate objective of the National
Population Policy is to address the unmet needs of contraception, health infrastructure, health personnel and to provide
integrated service delivery for basic reproductive and child health care.  The medium term objective is to bring the total
fertility rates to replacement level by 2010 through vigorous implementation of intersectoral operational strategies. The
long term objective is to achieve a stable population by 2045, at a level consistent with the requirement of sustainable
economic growth, social development and environmental protection.
