like agriculture-related vocational subjects which include repairing of pump sets, agricultural machines/implements etc. Similarly, fisheries can also be given
due attention.  Small trades like TV Mechanic and Radio can also generate employment in rural areas and these courses can also be incorporated under the
Scheme.  The Committee is of the view that in urban areas there are greater number of industries and job facilities and the industrial units should be linked to
the courses offered which can take into account the requirements of the industrial units.  If this is done, larger number of students including drop-outs can be
accommodated after the completion of their courses in the jobs of the industrial units.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that such trades be considered
for differential needs of urban and rural areas.  The Committee, in this connection, takes note of the Pre-Vocational course which is being implemented.  But it
is going at a snail’s pace and is required to beaccelerated.  This scheme may also be modified slightly to establish proper linkage with the main scheme.
Action Taken
National Policy on Education (NPE) 1986 provides for vocational education as a distinct stream intended to prepare students for identified occupations
spanning several areas of activity.  These courses should ordinarily be provided after the secondary stage, but flexibility has been provided to start Vocational
Education after Class-VIII.  Accordingly, there is no hindrance in starting vocational education programme after class VIII also.  The emphasis on
diversification to vocational education should only be after ten years of schooling is based on the minimum level of general education required to change from
childhood to adulthood.  Pre-vocational courses, which are generic, are being imparted in classes IX and X.  There already exist Community Polytechnics
wherein training is given in skills without insisting on formal qualifications.  In addition, Industrial Training Institutes are offering some of the trades for those
who have qualified up to 8
th standard.  National Open School (NOS) also provides to the school dropouts and disadvantaged groups through 6 months and 1
year vocational courses in seven broad disciplines like Radio & TV engineering, Electrical, technician course, refrigeration, librarianship, etc.
Further Recommendation
            The Committee is constrained to observe that the basic purpose of Vocational Education i.e. to provide skilled knowledge to earn livelihood through
works has not helped the Drop outs to a great extent.   The Committee is of the view that there is a need for greater coordination between Industry-Institute and
also need-based courses to be developed.   
Recommendation
2.15     The Committee is also constrained to note that lack of trained teachers is one of the weakest links.  The Committee desires that the States should be
asked to give priority to teachers’ training as this programme cannot be  successful without trained teachers.  The Committee is also concerned on the lack of
willingness on the part of the old teaching staff to accommodate new courses which stand as a stumbling block in the progress of Vocational Education.
Students are attracted only when new and up-to-date courses are offered.  The Committee feels that there is an urgency of Reorientation Training for existing
teachers to adapt themselves to new courses and also induction of more new teachers for updated courses.  However, the Committee feels that an element of
indecisiveness with regard to continuance of this scheme as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme persists.  This has created a sense of scepticism in the minds of the
State authorities implementing this scheme.  That is why teachers taken under this scheme are given only an ad-hoc appointment.  In this respect, the
Committee is of the view that once the teachers are appointed on a permanent basis, they would be actively involved in the training programmes offered.  In
this way, the Teachers training would be more meaningful.  The Committee is of the opinion that by this course of action the unemployment problem can be
solved to some extent.
Action Taken
            The status with regard to discontinuation of the scheme by the Centre and its transfer to States has since been removed in consultation with Planning
Commission and accordingly grants are now being released to States for expansion of the Scheme.  Some of the vocational courses have been updated and
courses on Information Technology have also been introduced in many States.  CBSE has introduced Vocational courses on Information Technology  from
Class X onwards.  Apart from the above, efforts have been made for training of more number of teachers by various Boards & PSSCIVE.  In an effort to be in
tune with times, encouragement of employed professionals as part-time teachers is being emphasised.  Visiting faculties, adjunct teachers from the industry/
corporates are also encouraged so that they bring  updated knowledge and new methodologies with them.
Further Recommendation
            The Committee understands that the fate of the Scheme is yet to be finally decided at the end of the 9
th Plan.  The Committee feels that implementation
of the scheme with all seriousness is not possible till a decision regarding the fate of the scheme is taken.  Though the Committee is inclined to be in agreement
with the engagement of part time professionals from Industry with the object of bringing updated information/technology to the scheme, the Committee has no
idea about the usefulness of this practice.  The Committee, therefore, opines that the idea of engaging outside professionals on part time basis for teaching
needs to be reviewed.  The Committee also reiterates its earlier observation of there being an urgent need for providing Re-orientation Training for existing
teachers to adapt themselves to new courses.
Recommendation
2.19     The Committee expresses concern over the under utilisation of the seats for the Apprenticeship training by vocational passouts. This has stood as a
weak link and has adversely affected the acceptability of the vocational trainees.  The Committee is of the opinion that steps must be taken to encourage the
students for going through Apprenticeship Training after completing Vocational Education which would make the Vocational Trainees more and more
acceptable to the industries.  There should be proper placement of students.  Hence, the Committee is of the view that the placement of students under
Apprenticeship Training needs to be vigorously implemented.  There should also be proper monitoring of it.
Action Taken
Central Apprenticeship Council has been advised to take up review of the guidelines with a view to accommodate more vocational pass-outs under the
apprenticeship programme.  Advance payment of stipends to apprentices and the industries is being contemplated.  This step is expected to make more and
more industries to volunteer for the apprenticeship programme.  A Co-ordination Committee under the chairmanship of Additional Secretary has been
constituted to review all issues related to implementation of the scheme including apprenticeship programme.
Further Recommendation
            The Committee hopes that the above exercise would be completed expeditiously, thereby leading to optimum utilization of seats for the Apprenticeship
training by Vocational passouts. 
Recommendation
2.20     The Committee has been given to understand that many Institutions running the vocational courses in the private and voluntary sectors make use of the
courses for financial exploitation and exorbitant fee is charged from the students.  Steps are, therefore, required to be taken to stop such exploitation and misuse
of vocational courses by the Management.
Action Taken
            Consequent to the inspections carried out during 1999-2000 some Non-Governmental Organisations were found to be non-performing.  As a result,
financial assistance to them have been restricted to the extent that only reputed organisations with innovative programmes are considered and extended
financial assistance.  Further, a copy of the sanction order is being endorsed to the local Panchayat, MLA, MP and concerned  state government, to keep a
watch over the functioning of these organisations.
Further Recommendation
            The Committee notes that in the inspections carried out during 1999-2000, some NGOs were found to be non-performing and action was taken against
them.  The Committee, however, is of the view that these inspections should be a regular feature.  Merely endorsement of sanction orders of NGOs to the local
Panchayat/MLA/MP and concerned State Govt. would not serve the purpose.  Area Officer should also be in touch with these authorities during his State visits
to get proper assessment of the functioning of a particular NGO.
Recommendation
2.22     The Committee has come to know that in the Chief Ministers’ Conference held in July, 1996, a decision was taken to transfer the scheme of Vocational
Education at +2 stage to the States.  However, as this decision has no endorsement of the National Development Council, the implementation of the scheme is
presently held up.  The Committee feels that this state of indecisiveness has adversely affected the scheme.  The Committee finds that Rs.60 crores were

were released to the States/UTs.  As a result, budget provision was brought down to Rs.20 crores and actual expenditure was only Rs.4 crores during 1997-98.

Further Recommendation
            The Committee understands that a final decision regarding the transfer of the scheme to States is yet to be taken by the Planning Commission.  This

Recommendation
2.24     The Committee is of the considered view that the Vocational Education Scheme is still continuing as a Pilot Project.  It has come to the notice of the
Committee that four external agencies/ institutions were entrusted the work of conducting a region-wise evaluation of the Vocational Education Scheme and
the final report has been submitted by Operation Research Group (ORG).  The Committee recommends that in the light of the findings of this report, the
States/UTs should be approached by the Deptt. for taking corrective measures for successful implementation of Vocational Education Scheme.
Action Taken
            Instructions have been issued to State/UT governments for taking corrective measures, such as to create proper management structure in the state for
proper monitoring of the implementation of the scheme.  In fact, the scheme is being extended for implementation during the Tenth plan period also.
     The Report of ORG was discussed by NCERT in its Working Group meeting held during 23-25 July, 1999.  In the Working Group State Government
representatives were also associated.
Further Recommendation
            The Committee recommends that the issues/findings of which there was consensus in the meeting of working group of NCERT should be
communicated to the States/UTs for implementation and followed up.
Recommendation
2.25     The Committee finds that at present a number of vocational schemes are being handled by different departments like  Education, Rural Employment
and Poverty Alleviation & Ministry of Labour.  However, Committee feels that there being no coordination among these Departments, achievement rate of
these schemes has not been quite satisfactory.  The Committee is, therefore, of the considered view that a common strategy should be evolved so as to integrate
all these Vocational Schemes and take the maximum advantage of the facilities available with the different departments.
Action Taken
            Representatives of other Central Government Departments like Agriculture, Health, Personnel and Training, etc. have been included in the Standing
Committee of the JCVE.
Further Recommendation
            The Committee is not convinced with the reply of the Department and reiterates its earlier recommendation.
Recommendation
2.26     The Committee observes that there has been regional disparity so far as setting up of ITI is  concerned.  Eastern region, Jammu & Kashmir and also the
Backward and Tribal areas are the most neglected lot.  The Committee feels that such areas need to be given special assistance.  The Committee, therefore,
recommends that steps should be initiated for provision of 100% Central Assistance for developing the institutional mechanism in these areas.  The Committee
finds that the organised sector has been the major beneficiary of ITIs.  The unorganised sector comprisingabout 90% of population mainly from rural areas
which also includes large number of Drop-outs and Non-Formal Education students has been totally left out.  This is due to the fact that there is a mismatch
between the labour market requirement and the trades and skills being offered in ITIs.  There being no proper outlet, average students are left with no
alternative but to opt for higher studies.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that urgent steps need to be taken for broad-basing the Vocational Education
Scheme by inducting area specific courses under I.T.Is.  
Action Taken
Efforts are underway to lay stress on area based and locally demand driven courses to benefit the rural youth and to reduce the regional disparity in
implementing the scheme.  For example, 516 Community Polytechnics, which are mostly located in rural areas conduct need based and locally demand driven
courses.  National Open School/State Open School also conducts courses throughout the country without insisting on formal qualifications.  In addition, Jana
Sikshan Sansthan, previously known as Shramik Vidya Peeth, also conducts vocational education programme.  Ministry of Labour has issued instructions to
the Directors of Industrial Training Institutes to allow their infrastructure to be used for vocational education purposes by the schools.
Further Recommendation
            The Committee feels that the present efforts on the part of the Department are not sufficient particularly with regard to balancing regional imbalances in
setting up technical institutes/ITIs in the country.  Although, 516 Community Polytechnics may be functioning in rural areas, but the Committee is conscious of
the fact that very few of them are located in backward, remote and hilly areas.  The Committee, is, therefore, of the view that such areas deserve special
attention in this regard.

REPORT
            I, the Chairman of the Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Hundred-
Eleventh Report of the Committee relating to the Cigarettes and other Tobacco Products (Prohibition of Advertisement
and Regulation of Trade and Commerce, Production, Supply and Distribution) Bill*, 2001. (please see Appendix-I)
2.         In pursuance of Rule 270 relating to the Department related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman,
Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha referred** the Bill, as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the
7th March, 2001 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and Report.
3.         As per the Statement of Objects and Reasons appended to the Bill, tobacco is universally regarded as one of the
major public health hazards and is responsible directly or indirectly for an estimated eight  lakh deaths annually in the
country.  It has also been stated that the treatment of tobacco related diseases and the loss of productivity caused thereby
cost the country almost Rs. 13,500  crores annually which more than offsets all the benefits accruing in the form of
revenue and employment generated by tobacco industry.  Keeping in view the seriousness of the problem and
recommendations of the Parliamentary Committee on Subordinate Legislation(10 thLok Sabha),  the need for a
comprehensive legislation to prohibit advertising and regulation of production, supply and distribution of cigarettes and
tobacco products was felt and a decision was taken to bring forward a suitable legislation in this regard.
4.         The Bill seeks to put total ban on advertising of cigarettes and other tobacco products and to prohibit
sponsorship of sports and cultural events, either directly or indirectly as well as sale of tobacco products to minors.   The
Bill also proposes to make rules for the purpose of prescribing the contents of the specified warnings, the languages in
which they are to be displayed, and displaying the quantities of nicotine and tar contents of these products.  The
objective of the proposed legislation is to reduce the exposure of people to tobacco smoke (passive smoking) and to
prevent the sale of tobacco products to minors and to protect them from becoming victims of misleading
advertisements.  It is hoped that this measure will result in a healthier lifestyle and the protection of right to life
enshrined in the Constitution.
5.         The Committee held eight-sittings, in all, to consider and finalise its report on the Bill.
6.         At its first meeting held on the 30
th May, 2001 the Committee discussed the Bill in general and sought

111th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/111threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:21]
clarifications on various allied aspects from the Secretary, Department of Health, Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare.  Having regard to the wider ramifications of the Bill,  it was decided to invite memoranda from individuals /
organizations / institutions etc. interested in the subject matter of the Bill.  For this purpose an advertisement was issued
in almost all the leading dailies of the country and wide publicity was also given through Doordarshan and All-India
Radio as well. (please see Appendix-II)
7.         The Committee received  55 memoranda containing suggestions and comments on various provisions of the Bill
from a number of  interested individuals, organizations, institutions, associations etc. (please see Appendix ‘III’ for the
list)  Representatives of a number of associations, trade unions, and also  NGOs, ex-MPs, appeared before the
Committee to air their views and also apprehensions on various aspects of the Bill. (please seeAppendix ‘IV’ for the
list).  Besides hearing the views of the Department of Health, the Committee also held interactions with representatives
of all the Departments/Ministries which are likely to be involved, directly or indirectly, in the implementation of various
provisions of the proposed Bill or likely to be affected after the Bill comes into force.
 
*Published in the Gazette of India Extraordinary Part-II, Section 2, dated the 7
th March, 2001.
**Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part-II dated the 12th March, 2001.
 
8.         Historically speaking, use of tobacco in one form or the other can be traced back to the 16
th century.  However,
it took nearly 400 years for the world to identify the life-taking diseases like cancer of different forms and various other
respiratory and cardiovascular diseases caused by the consumption of tobacco.  The medical science identified tobacco
as the single major cause of mortality and morbidity all over the world.  Smoking alone accounts for the highest death
rate in the age group of 35-64 years i.e. about 30 per cent for men and 22 per cent for women and is responsible for
roughly 3 million deaths annually.            Toxicity in the smoke emitted by the cigarettes is so menacing that all persons
around including children and the elderly persons, despite being non-smokers, are compelled to consume the smoke
without even knowing that the smoke that they are inhaling is gradually putting their own life into jeopardy.  The effect
of other tobacco products like beedies, cigars, paan masala, gutka, chewing tobacco has been found to be equally
harmful.  Estimates of persons suffering from cancer, coronary heart diseases and chronic obstructive lung disease on
account of tobacco use suggest that in India, there are about 1.41 lakh persons suffering on account of different types of
cancer of which one-third are women, about 43 lakh persons are suffering from coronary artery disease and another 40
lakh suffering from obstructive lung disease.   What  is a cause of serious concern is that treatment and management of
these three diseases is extremely resource intensive,necessitating substantial diversion  of resources available within the
country whether in the private or public domain. 
9.         In view of the adverse impact of tobacco on health, all the member countries of World Health Organization
(WHO) resolved to implement tobacco control through legislative means and increase public awareness.  So far, 133
countries have enacted legislation to discourage tobacco consumption and out of these, 128 countries have imposed a
ban in one form or the other on advertisement of tobacco products and many of them have made it compulsory for the
tobacco product manufacturers to indicate the nicotine and tar content on the packages.  The Committee has been
informed that a comprehensive anti-tobacco legislation is reported to have been found to be effective as countries with
stronger controls on advertising have recorded a lower consumption of tobacco. 
10.       In order to deal with the enormity of health hazards caused by tobacco, Government decided to regulate its
consumption through legislative means and brought forward the Cigarettes (Regulation of Production, Supply and
Distribution) Act in  1975 which, inter alia, made it mandatory to display a statutory warning “Cigarette smoking is
injurious to health” on all packages of cigarettes and in all advertisements. Another step in this direction was taken in
the year 1990 through an executive instruction of the Cabinet Secretariat through which smoking was prohibited at
certain public places like hospitals, dispensaries, educational institutions, conference rooms, domestic air flights, AC
sleeper coaches in trains, etc.
11.       In view of the need felt from time to time and the international experience gained in this regard, the Ministry of
Health and Family Welfare formulated a strategy for reducing the use of tobacco through an anti-tobacco legislation. 
After approval by the Committee of Secretaries on 10
th August, 1992, the proposal was submitted to the Cabinet
recommending the replacement of the Cigarettes(Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 1975 by a

111th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/111threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:21]
more comprehensive anti-tobacco legislation which would, inter alia, provide for a complete ban on all forms of
advertisements in respect of all tobacco products, a statutory warning including information on the nicotine and tar
content on all packages of tobacco and tobacco products in a more prominent manner, prohibition of sale of tobacco or
tobacco products within a distance of 100 meters from educational institutions / hospitals and ban on tobacco smoking
at public places.  The Cabinet at its meeting held on 24 th September, 1993 approved the proposal for drafting a Bill in
this regard.
12.       Meanwhile, in February, 1995, the Parliamentary Committee on Subordinate Legislation (10 th Lok Sabha)
examined the rules and regulations framed under the Cigarettes(Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution) Act,
1975.  The Committee during its deliberations took cognizance of the fact that the Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare was in the process of bringing out a comprehensive legislation on “Prohibition of Advertising and Regulation
of Production, Supply and Distribution of Tobacco Products”.  The Committee in its 22
nd Report presented to the Lok
Sabha on 22nd December, 1995 made a series of recommendations which were examined by a Coordination Committee
comprising representatives from the Ministry of Commerce, Agriculture, Labour, Information and Broadcasting, Indian
Council of Medical Research and NCERT.  While most of the Ministries agreed with the recommendations of the
Committee, the Ministry of Labour was of the view that the adverse impact of such a legislation on the livelihood of
labour force involved in tobacco production, processing and marketing could not be ignored.  Thereafter, comments and
reactions of all the concerned Ministries were obtained on the draft Cabinet note which was approved by the Cabinet at
its meeting held on the 6
th February, 2001.  After approval by the Cabinet, the present Bill was introduced in the Rajya
Sabha on 7th March, 2001.
13.       The Committee before finalizing its report on the Bill considered various memoranda, papers / documents placed
before it and the views expressed by the witnesses on the Bill.
14.       The Committee considered and adopted the report at its meeting held on 2
nd November, 2001.
15.       The recommendations / observations of the Committee with regard to the principal changes proposed in the Bill
are given below :-
Legislative competence of Parliament relating to the Bill :
15.1     The Bill contains restrictive provisions governing cigarettes as well as other tobacco products.   However, as per
clause 1 (2) of the Bill, after enactment, it will extend to the whole of India in respect of cigarettes alone.   Provisions
relating to other tobacco products will be made applicable, in the first instance, to the States of Goa, Punjab, Uttar
Pradesh and West Bengal, which have adopted the proposed legislation in pursuance of Clause (1) of Article 252 of the
Constitution and also to the Union Territories. Provisions relating to other tobacco products  can be made applicable to
the other States only after they adopt this Act by a Resolution passed in that behalf in pursuance of Clause(I) of Article
252 of the Constitution.  In other words, the Bill cannot be made applicable in the entire country as far as other tobacco
products are concerned, as in the case of cigarettes.           
15.2     During the course of its discussions and interaction with witnesses, one view point which emerged was that
when Parliament is competent to legislate on cigarettes, it should be equally competent to legislate on matters relating to
other tobacco products, both being health hazards.  It was pointed out that the proposed legislation seemed to be
discriminatory in nature because of its restricted applicability in respect of tobacco  products when compared with
cigarettes.   Such a situation was uncalled for specially in view of the consumption pattern prevalent in our country.  
Whereas tobacco in othercountries is synonymous with cigarettes, in our country bulk of tobacco consumption, i.e. 84%
is in the from of beedis and chewing tobacco/gutka etc., cigarettes accounting for merely 16%
15.3     When asked to comment on this view point during the course of the meeting of the Committee held on the 30
th
May, 2001, the Secretary, Department of Health clarified that Government intended to create an umbrella legislation
which was not automatically binding on the State Governments statutorily for other tobacco products, but which could
be adopted later on if State legislature felt the need for same.   He informed the Committee that  legal opinion in this
regard was obtained from the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs.   Legal position as clarified by the
Ministry of law, Justice and Company Affairs  (Department of Legal Affairs) in 1997 is as follows:-
 “The law relating to production, supply and distribution of industrial products can be made under Entry 26 of the State
List or Entry 33 of the Concurrent List of the VII schedule of the Constitution of India.  Under Entry 33, Parliament

111th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/111threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:21]
may enact a law in respect of those industries which are controlled industries under Entry 52 of List 1.  Cigarette
Industry has been included as item 38(1) of the First Schedule of Industries (Development andRegulation) Act, 1952. 
Parliament is, therefore, competent to enact a law relating to cigarettes and not for other forms of tobacco products
which are within the jurisdiction of the State Legislature.
            However, in view of the provisions contained in Article 252 (1) of the Constitution of India, Parliament would
be competent to enact law in respect of tobacco products for those States which adopt the law passed by the Parliament
by adopting a Resolution by the House of the State or where there are two Houses by each of the Houses of the
Legislature of that State.  The State Legislature of Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Goa and Punjab have passed Resolution
to adopt Central Government Legislation on the subject”.
15.4     However, one of the witnesses who appeared before the Committee in its meeting held on 3
rd July, 2001
advocated that Parliament has given the Union jurisdiction over all tobacco products by virtue  of section 2 of the
Tobacco Board Act, 1975 which reads as follows:-
"It is hereby declared that it is expedient in the public interest that the Union should take under its control the tobacco
industry”.
15.5     The above provision was incorporated under Entry 52 of List I (Union List) of the Seventh Schedule of the
Constitution under which Parliament can make law relating to industries the control of which by the Union is declared
by Parliament by law to be expedient in the public interest.   It was thus not necessary for Parliament to receive
Resolutions from the States under Article 252 (1) of the Constitution authorising Parliament to pass an Act in this
behalf.  
15.6     Committee's attention was also drawn to the Supreme Court Judgement in thecase of ITC and Others Vs. State of
Karnataka and Others 1985 (Supp) SCC 476 whereby Supreme Court has ruled  that the entire tobacco industry stands
under the control of Union as a consequence of the Tobacco Board Act, 1975.
15.7     Because of raising of legal issues regarding the legislative competence of Parliament relating to the Bill,  the
Committee decided to seek the opinion of Department of Legal Affairs in the Ministry of Law, Justice & Company
Affairs in the matter.  The Department of Legal Affairs in its opinion dated 24
th August, 2001 stated as under:-
“It is true that while enacting the Tobacco Board Act, 1975, a parliamentary declaration as envisaged under entry 52 of
the Union List was made in Section 2 thereof to the effect that it is expedient in the public interest that the Union should
take under its control the tobacco industry.  Nevertheless, the vital question is whether by virtue of that control, the
Parliament can legislate regarding trade and commerce in, and the production, supply and distribution of other tobacco
products and as also on aspects such as prohibition of smoking in public places and prohibition of advertisement of
tobacco products and to provide for statutory warning about harmful effects of smoking / consumption of other tobacco
products.  The answer to this question would depend on the extent of the control of tobacco industry taken over by the
Union under the Tobacco Board Act, 1975.  As it would appear from the long title of the Act, the Act was enacted to
bring development of the tobacco industry under the control of the Union.  The Act provides for setting up of Tobacco
Board for that purpose.  The Board regulates the production / plantation and disposal of Virginia tobacco.  That apart, it
also authorizes the Central Government to make provision for prohibiting, restricting or otherwise controlling the import
and export of tobacco and tobacco products.  Thus, it would appear that all the objectives of the present Bill are not
covered by the Tobacco Board Act, 1975.  The contents and scope of the Tobacco Board Act and the present Bill are
different.  In the absence of a separate declaration as envisaged under entry 52 of the Union List, it may be open to
challenge, if the applicability of the proposed law as regards other tobacco products is extended to the whole of India.  
Therefore, the Bill seeks to extend the proposed law only to those States, namely, Goa, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, West
Bengal in the first instance, legislatures of which have passed resolution under Article 252 of the Constitution. In other
words, in the absence of such a declaration, the Parliament appears to have competence to make law regarding other
tobacco products for the purposes mentioned in the Bill only for the States, the legislatures of which have passed
resolutions under Article 252 of the Constitution authorizing Parliament to make law.”
15.8     The Department further stated ¾
“It would not be out of place to mention that the 39
th World Health Assembly meeting held in Geneva in May, 1996 had
passed a Resolution ‘Tobacco & Health’ whereby it confers tobacco smoking and use of tobacco in any of its form is on
attainment of ‘Health for All’ by the year 2000 AD.  That resolution also urged the member States to implement tobacco

111th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/111threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:21]
control strategies through legislative means and increased public awareness.  This resolution also enables Parliament to
make law for the whole or any part of territory of India for implementing any treaty, agreement or convention with any
country or countries or any decision made at any international conference, association or other body.   For the purposes
of present Bill, the above resolution was not, however, invoked.” 
15.9     The Department of Legal Affairs has opined that whether Parliament’s jurisdiction may be assumed by making a
separate declaration under entry 52 of the Union List for the purpose of extending the applicability of the proposed law
to the whole of India in respect of other tobacco products is a matter of policy.  If such a declaration is decided to be
made under entry 52 of the Union List specifically identifying other tobacco products, i.e. other tobacco industries, the
Parliament would have jurisdiction to make law in respect of products of such tobacco industries even in the absence of
resolution of State Legislatures under Article 252 of the Constitution.   According to the Department, in that event it
would also be advisable to utilize the resolution passed by World Health Assembly in May, 1986 so as to avoid any
possible attack on Parliament’s competence to make law relating to aspects concerning health which are otherwise
covered under entry 6 of the State List. 
15.10   The Committee also heard the Secretaries in the Departments of Health and Legal Affairs for further
clarification in the matter at its meeting held on the 16
th October, 2001. The Committee fails to understand as to why the
Supreme Court Judgement and World Health Assembly Resolution were not taken into account while deciding the
legislative competence of Parliament in the context of the present Bill.  Contention of the Department of Health that in 
Constitutional matters, they rely completely  on the advice given by the Ministry of Law does not seem to be fully
convincing.    The Committee is also not inclined to agree with the impression given by the Department of Health that
World Health Assembly Resolutions, being recommendatory in nature, can not be treated as international obligations.  
There is also no doubt that final decision in the matter of Parliament's jurisdiction in the present case which is a policy
issue is to be decided by the Government,   but the fact remains that comprehensive advice inclusive of all the relevant
aspects should have been given by the Ministry of Law in the first instance itself.
15.11   The Committee feels that the Bill in its present form makes discrimination between cigarettes and other tobacco
products and also discriminates amongst their users. While the smokers of cigarettes will be restricted throughout the
country, the users of other tobacco products will have no restriction at all in the States where the proposed legislation
may not be adopted.  The Committee, therefore, asked the Secretaries to submit a draft of the clause enabling Parliament
to legislate on all tobacco products, for its consideration. 
15.12   The Committee considered the draft clause submitted by the concerned departments and recommends that the
Preamble to the Bill may be replaced as under :- 
“Whereas, the Resolution passed by the 39
th World Health Assembly (WHO), in its Fourteenth Plenary meeting held on
the 15th May, 1986 urged the Member States of WHO which have not yet done so  to implement the measures to ensure
that effective protection is provided to non-smokers  from involuntary exposure to tobacco smoke and to protect
children and young people from being addicted to the use of tobacco;
            And whereas, the 43 rd World Health Assembly in its Fourteenth Plenary meeting held on the 17 th May, 1990,
reiterated the concerns expressed in the Resolution passed in the 39th World Health Assembly and urged Member States
to consider in their tobacco control strategies  plans for legislation and other effective measures for protecting their
citizens with special attention to risk groups such as pregnant women and children  from involuntary exposure to
tobacco smoke,  discourage the use of tobacco and impose progressive restrictions and take concerted action to
eventually eliminate all direct and indirect advertising, promotion and sponsorship concerning tobacco;
And whereas, India is a signatory to the above said Resolutions and it is considered necessary to implement the
said Resolutions and in pursuance of Article 253 of the Constitution;
            And whereas, it is considered expedient to enact a comprehensive law  on tobacco control in the public interest
and to protect the public health;
            And whereas, it is expedient to prohibit the consumption of cigarettes and other tobacco products which are

Affairs to be incorporated in the present Bill also.
15.14   The Committee also recommends that consequential changes necessitated by incorporation of the above
provision in the Bill may also be carried out where necessary. 
Clause 2 :
15.15   This clause defines various expressions used in the Bill.  Sub-clause (l) of this clause provides definition of the
expression “Public Place”.  The Committee recommends that under this definition Railway Waiting Room may also be
included.
Clause 6 :
15.16   This clause puts restrictions on trade and commerce in and production, supply and distribution of cigarettes and
other tobacco products.  As per sub-clause (1) of this clause, indication of specified warning has been made compulsory
on every package of cigarettes or any other tobacco products.  The Committee recommends that besides written
warning, some symbol like skull, cross bones or any suitable pictorial depiction may also be given specially for the
convenience of illiterate or semi literate consumers.
15.17   As per sub-clause(5) of this clause, indication of nicotine and tar contents has been made compulsory for
cigarettes.  However,  it exempts other tobacco products from this requirement.  The Committee is of the view that
nicotine and tar content present either in cigarettes or beedis or in other tobacco products make no discrimination in
terms of causing injury to human body. The Committee apprehends that by requiring only cigarettes to declare nicotine
and tar contents will create the impression that other tobacco products do not contain such substances and are, therefore,
less harmful.  This perception could result in consumption shifting away from cigarettes to other tobacco products. It,
therefore, recommends that printing of nicotine and tar contents as well as maximum permissible limit thereof on
packets and cartons of all tobacco products be made compulsory.   The Committee also recommends that consequential
changes necessitated by the above change may also be carried out in the relevant provisions of the Bill. 
Clauses 15, 20 and 22 :
15.18   Clause 15 provides for penalty not exceeding five times the value of the package of cigarettes or of any other
tobacco products of Rupees one thousand whichever is more  where specified warning is not contained on package of
cigarettes and other tobacco products and contents of nicotine and tar are not indicated on package of cigarettes.  Clause
20, for the same offence,  prescribes imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or with fine which may
extend to one lakh rupees or with both in the case of first conviction and imprisonment for a term which may extend to
three years or with fine which may extend to two lakh rupees or with both in the case of second or subsequent
conviction. 
15.19   The Committee feels that clauses 15 and 20 provide different sets of punishment  for the same offence  which
will be against the principle of natural justice.   It, therefore, recommends that these two clauses may be combined
together.  The Committee also finds that punishment for both the producer and the seller is the same.  In this connection,
the Committee notes that cigarettes and other tobacco products come to the retailer for sale in the package form.  The
main responsibility for ensuring the specified warning and/or indication of nicotine and tar content on the package of
cigarettes and other tobacco products is that of the producer or manufacturer and not the seller.  Moreover, a seller of
these products is generally a poor and illiterate or semi-literate person who does not possess the capability to read and
understand the nuances of nicotine and tar content. The Committee, therefore, is of the considered view that there

111th Report

should be different penalties for producers /manufacturers  and sellers of cigarettes and other tobacco products. 
15.20 Clause 22provides punishment for advertisement of tobacco products.  As per this clause a person shall be
punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or with fine which may extend to one lakh
rupees for contravening the provision of section 4 in the case of first conviction.  For the second and subsequent
conviction the penalty would be imprisonment upto three years or with fine which may extend to Rs. two lakhs or both. 
15.21   The Committee also observes that punishment for failure to give specified warning, nicotine and tar content and
advertisement of tobacco products as prescribed in clauses 20 and 22 seem to be excessive and disproportionate when
compared to penalties prescribed for much more serious offences.  For example, under section 275 of Indian Penal Code
(IPC) punishment for sale of adulterated drugs is 6 months imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1000/-.  For the attempt to
commit culpable homicide,  section 308 of IPC prescribes imprisonment for 3 years or fine or both.  The Committee
strongly feels that penalties prescribed in clauses 20 and 22 will create unnecessary and unjustified harassment specially
for petty  traders, retailers and hawkers as well as increase the scope for  corruption.  The Committee, therefore,
recommends that provisions of clauses 20 and 22 need to be reviewed in the light of punishments provided in
comparable legislations.
Clause 25
15.22   This clause relates to prevention, detention and place of trial of offences under sections 3 and 5.  Clause 25(2)
empowers a police officer or any officer of the State Government, not below the rank of Sub-Inspector of Police, to
arrest any person without warrant when he has reasonable ground to believe that such person has committed an offence
under section 3 or section 5.  The Committee feels that given the nature of offence contemplated under section 3 or
section 5, arresting anyone without warrant or on mere apprehension that he might have violated the provisions of these
sections is very harsh.  The Committee also apprehends that bestowing of such blanket power on the officer of the rank
of Sub-Inspector of Police may become a tool of exploitation.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that there should
not be any provision for arrest without proper warrant in case of  violation of the provisions of section 3 or section 5. 
15.23   The Committee is in agreement with other provisions of the Bill.
16        General
The Committee has been given to understand that if a person is kept away from tobacco for the first twenty years
of his life, there is a very high probability that he will remain tobacco free for rest of his life.  Hence, it is mostly the
teenagers and young school or college going students who are most vulnerable to the addiction of tobacco.  The
Committee is, therefore, of the view that  availability of cigarette and other tobacco products should be made difficult
for these age groups of people.  As a first step, the Committee feels that sale of cigarettes and tobacco products should
be completely banned within a radius of five hundred yards of educational institutions and therefore, recommends
making a suitable provision to this effect in the Bill. 
17        General Recommendations and Observations :
17.1     The Committee, besides recommending amendments to various clauses of the Bill, wishes to make certain
general recommendations and observations which though not directly related to the Bill, may have consequential effect
in different spheres.  It will be necessary to address those issues while bringing in this legislation.  Some of the issues
which the Committee feels,  need to be addressed, are given below:
Farmers and workers
17.2     The Committee had the opportunity to interact with a number of associations representing tobacco farmers and
growers and various trade unions.  By and large, there was support for the Bill as a safeguard for public health. 
However, the Committee noticed that there was deep apprehension on its likely impact on the employment scenario in
the tobacco sector.  It was repeatedly pointed out to the Committee that as a result of ban on advertisements and sale of
tobacco products and various other restrictions proposed in the Bill, the demand for such products would decline
thereby adversely affecting the production of tobacco and tobacco products resulting in loss of employment and
livelihood to millions of farmers and workers presently engaged in tobacco sector.
Import of cigarettes 
17.3     The Committee has been given to understand that domestic cigarette industry is suffering heavily due to the
present import policy of the Government.  The Committee notes that cigarette is a bound item and as per the WTO

111th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/111threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:21]
resolution a maximum import duty of 150% can be levied. However, in India the present import duty on cigarette is
only 35%   which is adversely affecting the domestic cigarette industry.  The Committee fails to understand the reason
behind keeping an import duty of only 35% on an item like cigarette, which is a known health hazard, when the same
can be increased upto 150% as per the WTO resolution.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the import duty on
cigarettes needs to be increased to the maximum admissible level so as to discourage its use on the one hand and
preventing the country from becoming the dumping ground of foreign cigarettes on the other. 
Smuggling of cigarettes 
17.4     The Committee was given to understand that the cigarette industry in the country has experienced an abnormal
increase in the availability of smuggled brands in recent years.  Situation has worsened with growing influx of low
priced brands, further eroding the domestic industry. Cartons of cigarettes land into the country as a duty-free item for
personal consumption which actually find their way in the market for sale at a higher premium. It was pointed out that
an unintended consequence of restrictions and regulations on the domestic cigarette industry as proposed in the present
Bill will be that contraband sales will get a further fillip.  The Committee finds this situation very serious and alarming
and opines that existing mechanism needs to be strengthened urgently  to check such kind of undesirable and illegal
activities in the country. 
Segregation in  hotels, restaurants and airports
17.5     The representatives of the Federation of Hotel and Restaurant Associations of India voiced their reservations
about ban on smoking in restaurants as envisaged in the proposed Bill.  Their contention was that such a move would
adversely affect the hotel industry as there was likelihood of decrease in the number of persons visiting hotels and
restaurants.  The Federation suggested to the Committee that a suitable provision could be incorporated in the Bill
providing for segregation of smoking and non-smoking areas in a restaurant/hotel which has a seating capacity of fifty
persons or more.   Similarly, a provision could be made for demarcating smoking and non-smoking zones in hotels
which have a capacity of fifty rooms or more.   The Federation also added that they were suggesting this because of the
fact that small hotel/restaurant owners might find it difficult to make necessary arrangement for segregation. 
Representatives of ASSOCHAM and CII also advocated flexibility in deciding smoking and non-smoking areas in
Airports besides hotels and restaurants.
17.6     The Committee having considered the issue in its entirety  recommends that a suitable provision may be
incorporated in the Bill so as to  provide for segregation of smoking and non-smoking area/space  in hotels/restaurants
having  a seating capacity of 30 persons or 30 rooms and also airports.
Advertisement through Media
17.7     The Committee has been given to understand that multinational cigarette companies have built extremely strong
brand appeals through sustained and massive advertising and promotional inputs over many decades.  A number of
witnesses who appeared before  the Committee were of the view that the advertising restrictions laid down in the
proposed Bill will lead to discrimination between domestic and foreign cigarette manufacturers.  While domestic
manufacturers will be prohibited from advertising, foreign cigarette MNCs will have the freedom to advertise on
satellite TV, foreign print media having a circulation in India and also on internet, thereby giving them an unfair
competitive advantage over Indian brands.  The Committee shares the apprehensions expressed by various associations.
17.8     The Committee discussed this issue with the Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.  The
Secretary informed the Committee  that presently there is only one Central Monitoring Service agency which monitors
foreign broadcasting.  This agency is very old and belongs to the eighties when most of the broadcasting was public
broadcasting.  The Committee feels that, at present, when most of the broadcasting is private and there are innumerable
private television and radio channels and new channels coming up every day, such an ill-equipped Central monitoring
service won’t be able to keep a constant tab on foreign and private channels.  The  Secretary admitted that presently they
do not have a system or a center which can monitor each and every channel, record the violation of domestic laws
therein and instruct the cable operator to stop transmitting that particular channel which is violating the law. The
Secretary informed the Committee that efforts would be made to include a scheme in the Tenth Plan whereby a fully
equipped monitoring mechanism is set up. 
17.9     The Committee recommends that the Centre and the States should constitute joint monitoring committees which
are equipped with state-of-the-art monitoring equipments so that in case of violation of any domestic law by any of the
channels, prompt action could be taken against them.  The Committee also feels that foreign TV channels that earn

advertising and distribution revenue in India, should be made accountable to ensure that they do not beam tobacco
advertising into the country. Besides that, there is also a need for having of suitable penal provision in the Bill for cable
TV operators if they transmit and promote tobacco advertisements through their network.
Social Awareness
17.10   The Committee is of the considered view that apart from Legislation,  an anti-tobacco campaign should be 
launched so as to make the people conscious of the ill effects of use of tobacco.   An atmosphere should be created in
which people give up the habit of tobacco consumption  voluntarily.   This would make the job of implementation of the
legislation easier and effective. The Committee feels that the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can play a very
effective role by developing ad films highlighting the ill-effects of tobacco consumption and broadcasting and televising
them on different channels on a regular basis.  Besides this, students in schools and colleges also need to be educated
through their curriculum as this section of society is considered to be the most vulnerable.

APPENDIX-II
 
Parliamentary Committee on Human Resource Development  invites suggestions on
the Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products (Prohibition of Advertisement and
Regulation of Trade and Commerce, Production, Supply and Distribution), Bill, 2001.
 
The Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products (Prohibition of Advertisement and Regulation of Trade and
Commerce, Production, Supply and Distribution), Bill, 2001.  as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 7 th March, 2001,
has been referred to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource Development, 
headed by Shri S.B. Chavan, M.P., for examination and report.
2.         The Bill seeks to put total ban on advertising of cigarettes and other tobacco products and to prohibit
sponsorship of sports and cultural events either directly or indirectly as well as sale of tobacco products to minors.   The
objective of the proposed enactment is to reduce the exposure of people to tobacco smoke (passive smoking) and to
prevent the sale of tobacco products to minors and to protect them from becoming victims of misleading
advertisements.    This will result in a healthier life style and protection of right to life as enshrined in the Constitution.
  The proposed legislation further seeks to implement article 47 of the Constitution which, inter alia, requires the State to
endeavour to improve public health of the people.
3.         In this connection, it has been decided to invite suggestions/comments from individuals,  organisations,
institutions, tobacco growers  etc. interested in the subject matter of the Bill.  Interested persons, organisations,
institutions, etc. can obtain copies of the Bill from the Committee Officer, Rajya Sabha Secretariat, Cabin `E’,
Basement, Parliament House Annexe, New Delhi – 110001.  Suggestions/Comments on the Bill can be sent  to Shri
C.B. Rai, Under Secretary, Rajya Sabha Secretariat, Parliament House Annexe (Room No. 539), New Delhi-110001
Telephone: 3034053) latest by 30
th  June, 2001.  Persons/Organisations who are interested to appear before the
Committee to express their views, besides written submission, may indicate so.

M.P.  in its meeting held on 6 th August, 1998  to look into the various aspects of the  Medical Education for making an
in-depth study on the subject and to present a report thereon to the Committee at an early date.
 
3.         The Sub-Committee, considered various documents and relevant papers received from the Department of
Health,  Ministry of Heath and Family Welfare and Medical Council of India on the subject.  The Committee also 
heard  the oral evidence of the Secretaries  of the Department of Health and Medical Council of India respectively and

 REPORT
I           INTRODUCTION
1.1       Role of medical education in a developing country like India is very important.   Nobody can deny the fact that
health care and medical education play a complimentary role.   For the effective implementation of all the National
Health Programmes, contribution of the teaching hospitals is very vital.   However, what is being observed is that
majority of young medical graduates opt  for urban hospitals and clinical practice, the trend towards specialization is
high, vacancies in rural health centres are on the increase, professional interest both at the level of practitioner and
educator continues to be in illness care at the secondary and tertiary level rather than in the challenges of primary health
care and public health.   The  increasing commercialization of medical education and erosion of norms in medical ethics
is also a  matter of serious concern.
1.2       Against this backdrop, the Committee on Human Resource Development appointed a Sub-Committee on
Medical Education on 6
th August, 1998 with the objective of assessing and analyzing the status of medical education in
the country from all conceivable angles.   However,  the Sub-Committee  had  to leave its task unfinished due to the
dissolution of 12th Lok Sabha.   Subsequently  a new Sub-Committee  was  appointed  on 26th May, 2000 which carried
forward the work of the previous Sub-Committee.
1.3       The Sub-Committee invited comments and suggestions from individuals, experts, doctors, medical teachers on
the status of medical education in the country through a Press Release issued on 18 th August, 1998.   An overwhelming
response was received from all over the country.   The Sub-Committee visited the States of Andhra Pradesh, Tamil
Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra and Union Territory of  Pondicherry to have a first-hand information on the
subject.   The Sub-Committee had the opportunity of  visiting medical colleges – both Govt. and Private and held
extensive and fruitful discussions with members of faculty and student community.   During these visits, the  Sub-
Committee also met a very large number of experts, medical professionals and Principals of  medical colleges which
could not be visited by it.  The Sub-Committee also held wide-ranging deliberations with State authorities to understand
their view-point on the subject.   Besides that, the Sub-Committee also visited AIIMS, Maulana Azad Medical College,
Lady Hardinge Medical College, University College of Medical Sciences and  ICMR in Delhi.   Representatives of PGI,
Chandigarh  were invited by the Sub-Committee to Delhi for knowing their views.   Due to time-constraint, it was not
possible for the Sub-Committee to visit any more State.   However, a detailed questionnaire was sent to all the Govt.
medical colleges in the remaining parts of the country and response from a large number of colleges was received.  
Besides that, State Govts  were also  requested to give their suggestions and quite a few State Govts  responded. 
Finally, the Committee heard the Secretary, MCI and  Secretary, Department of Health on 17
th July and 14th September,
2001.    The Committee shared its impressions/experiences with them and sought clarifications on various aspects of
medical education in the country.
II          OVERVIEW

112th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/112threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:22]
2.1       It has been observed  that there has been a rapid increase in the   number  of medical colleges during the last two
decades with the maximum number  of colleges coming up in Southern and Western parts of the country.   The present
number of medical colleges in the country is 183, ( vide Annexure ) out of which 69 are private medical colleges. 
Mushrooming  of medical colleges has led to a  situation of regional imbalance  as very few medical colleges have come
up in northern states and the North Eastern region is almost bereft of  this  facility.   The Committee has been given to
understand that  contribution from the private sector notwithstanding, mushrooming of private medical colleges
continued to flourish with the tacit  support of State Govts for a considerable  period.   The Committee observes that the
amendments made in the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 in 1993 by laying down very stringent norms for
establishment of new medical college, increase in the intake capacity and introduction of a new or higher course of
study  has  checked   the mushroom growth of  medical colleges in the country to some extent.   However, these norms
need to be enforced uniformly  and  with an objective approach.   Sporadic proposals for starting a very large number of
medical colleges at a stroke  still continue to be noticed.
2.2       The Committee had the opportunity to visit both Govt and private medical  colleges and interact with the
management, faculty members and student representatives.   Feedback with regard to  functioning of both Govt. and 
private  medical colleges was also received from different quarters.   While it is true that  common parameters about the 
two categories of medical colleges can not be drawn, the Committee  has the following observations to make.  Private
medical colleges, in the initial period, barely reach the standards and  norms set up by MCI  with regard to
infrastructure, manpower etc.   Similarly, in the Govt. medical  colleges set up in different parts of the country, with the
passage of time there has been a steady deterioration in the infrastructure because of   inability of State Govts  to
provide any assistance  whatsoever due to their very poor financial position.   Other major   constraints noticed in the
smooth functioning of Govt. medical colleges are control of too many authorities, lack of accountability, prolonged
procedure of recruitment  and promotion of teachers.   Inadequate  staff, unwarranted interference by management and
manipulation in the admission of students can be said to be major drawbacks of private medical colleges.    The
Committee also noticed that access to clinical facilities having large patient attendance was there in Govt. medical
colleges.   In contrast in private medical colleges, in spite of having impressive      hospital  buildings, required clinical
material  was lacking.
III        MEDICAL COUNCIL OF INDIA (MCI)
3.1       Medical Council of India (MCI) is a statutory body which was established under the  Indian Medical Council
Act, 1956.   It is a nodal body assigned the task of processing the proposals for establishment of a new medical college,
starting  of a new or higher course of study or training and increasing of admission capacity in any course of study  or
training.      Other major function  of MCI is regulating the standard of medical education by carrying out regular
inspections of different medical colleges  located all over the country in accordance with the  provisions of the Act and
Regulations made thereunder.    The Council is also empowered to recommend withdrawal of recognition in respect of
any college based on its inspections.   Thus, it can be said  that MCI acts as the watchdog  for maintaining  the standard
of medical education in the country.
3.2       MCI is composed of both elected and nominated members.   As laid down in Section 3(1) of the IMC Act, 1956
under the elected category, one member of the medical faculty from each university, one member from each State in
which a State Medical  Register is maintained and seven members to be elected  from amongst themselves by persons
enrolled on any of the State Medical Registers are included.   Under the nominated category, one member from each
state is nominated by the Central Govt. in  consultation with the State Govt.  and eight members are to be nominated by
the  Central Govt.   Thus,  composition of MCI was envisaged to be well represented having members from all the
required  categories.
3.3       The Committee has been informed that  as on 21
st June, 2001, the  total membership of MCI is 113 out of which
77 are filled  up and 36 are vacant.   Out of 77 members in position, 34 belong to the nominated category and 43 are
from the elected category.    Out of the total number of 36 vacancies, 35 are from the  elected category.   The Committee
observes that the  present composition of  MCI cannot be said  to be of an All India  character.   This is all the more
evident as only  fifteen members form the quorum  of the Council and all the acts of the Council are   decided by a
majority of the members present and voting.
3.4       The Committee notes that out of 36 vacancies in the  113-member Council, 21 are in the seats reserved for
Universities.  Reason for vacancies in this category, as intimated by    the Department is non-constitution/non-

112th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/112threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:22]
reconstitution  of Senate or Court of the Universities or  meetings of the Senate/Court not being held for a long time.   
What is a cause of  serious concern  is that Universities are simply not responding to the reminders  sent by the Council
and the Central Govt. from time to time and vacancies are continuing in some cases for the last 10-15 years.
3.5       In some states, a number of Universities now fall under the jurisdiction of Health Universities  established in the
recent years.   This development has led to a peculiar situation.   By virtue of coming under the jurisdiction of a Health
University, such Universities   have lost their right of being represented in the Council.   On the other hand, Health
Universities  cannot send their nominee to the  Council as they do not have any Senate.   Thus, as many as 21
Universities over and above 56 eligible Universities are not represented in the Council.   Health Universities   having a 
large number of medical colleges under their  jurisdiction, specially  in southern  and western states have no say in the
decision-making apex body on medical education.
3.6       Out of 15 seats representing the Registered Medical Graduates (RMG) Constituency, 7 are lying vacant for
varying periods of time.   The Committee has been informed that the  main reason for vacancies   in this category is that
Returning Officers who are quite often the Registrar, State Medical Council or the State Director of Medical Education,
keep on changing due to change of incumbents  and in some cases voters’ list has not been prepared up-to-date.   The
Committee is constrained to observe that in spite of funds towards expenses for conducting the  election being provided
by the Council, the Returning Officers  are simply not responding to the reminders of the  Council.
3.7       Situation is equally disturbing so far as seats representing Licentiate Group are concerned.   At present, all the
seats are lying vacant.   The Committee  has been given to understand that Asstt. Director General, Directorate General
of Health Services was appointed as the Returning Officer on 21
st January,1997.   However, as late as on 12 th June,
2000, the Assistant Director-General approached the Central Govt. with a   request to be spared from the responsibilities
of Returning Officer due to his transfer to Lady Hardinge Medical College.  Thereafter,  ADG of Health Services was
appointed as the Returning Officer w.e.f. 19 th June, 2000.   It  has been informed that he has so far received lists of
registered licentiates from 12 State Medical Councils and the remaining 6 State  Medical Councils have also been
reminded.   The Committee feels that chances of election process being completed in the near future seem to be very
dim.
3.8       The Committee is of the strong opinion that procedure for election of different categories of  posts to the Council
is too rigid.   There is an urgent need for streamlining  the election procedure, more so, if the representative composition
of the Council as envisaged in the IMC Act, 1956 is sought to be maintained.   The Committee has been given to
understand that a proposal of the Council for bringing out amendment in the relevant provisions of the Indian Medical
Council Rules, 1957 for expediting election of members from Medical Faculty of Universities is pending with the
Central Govt.  since 15
th February, 1999.    The Committee recommends that the Central Govt. should take immediate
steps in the matter.   The Committee would also urge upon the Central Govt. to take up the issue of non-completion of
election process for other categories of seats with the concerned State Govts and impress upon them  to expedite the
same.   The Committee recommends that the Central Govt. should review the various provisions for constituting the
Council laid down in the Act and the Regulations made thereunder for removing the anomalies therein.
3.9       A basic problem in the  MCI structure is that since education is a State subject, it has in principle only  a
recommendatory role, not a regulatory one.  In the  absence of regulatory powers, MCI’s ability to maintain standards
has been severely compromised by State Govts/private medical colleges.   The Committee has been given to understand
that although with the amendment of IMC Act in 1993, sufficient powers have been vested with MCI so as to supervise
the maintenance of  standard of  education in medical colleges across the country, it has not proved to be effective.
3.10     The Council explained that minimum requirements in respect of staff, infrastructure, equipment etc as prescribed
in various Regulations are being checked periodically through inspections.  So far the Council  has not found any
difficulty in implementing its regulations and warnings given to medical college authorities for removal of deficiencies
have proved to be effective.
3.11     The Committee is not inclined to agree with the viewpoint  of the Council.  In its all the study visits  and
interactions with the various   functionaries comprising the entire medical education   spectrum, one view  that has been
consistently put across before the Committee, was that with the increase  in the number of medical colleges over the
years, it is practically not possible for a centralized body like MCI to constantly monitor the standard of medical
education.    The Committee observes that there is no regional council of the MCI.   The State  Medical Councils are
autonomous bodies established by State Govts that too not by all the State Govts.    These  State Medical Councils have

112th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/112threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:15:22]
no   authority in the maintenance of standards of medical education.   In such a  scenario with 183   medical colleges
spread across the country with chances  of future expansion, the Committee strongly feels that regional  councils  with
MCI continuing as the apex body need to be set up in the country.   The Committee is of the view that both the Central
Govt. and MCI should explore the possibility of setting up four regional councils  in  Southern, Northern, Eastern and
Western parts of the country.   This would ultimately lead to better monitoring of the standard of medical  education as
laid down in the IMC Act, 1956  and Regulations made thereunder.     The Committee also desires that the Department
may take up the matter of establishing  State Medical Council in the States where they are not existing.   Role of State
Medical Council may also be reviewed so as to involve them in the exercise of maintaining the standards of Medical
Education in the States under the guidance of MCI.
IV        PROCEDURE/NORMS PRESCRIBED FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF A MEDICAL COLLEGE, STARTING
A NEW  OR HIGHER COURSE OF STUDY OR TRAINING AND INCREASING THE ADMISSION CAPACITY
4.1       Section 10A of the IMC Act, 1956 deals with the procedure for obtaining permission for establishment of a  new
medical college, starting a new or higher course of study or training and  increasing the admission capacity. There also
exist Minimum Standard Requirements for a Medical College for 50 admissions  annually Regulations, 1999 and similar
regulations for 100 admissions and 150 admissions separately.   These regulations provide  for a specific area
requirement for various departments both in the medical colleges and teaching hospitals, staff strength required and
equipment for various departments.  
4.2       By and large, the feedback which the Committee received with regard to the procedure and various
norms/conditions prescribed for opening a new medical college, starting a new course and increasing the intake capacity
emphasized their efficacy and necessity for checking the mushroom growth of medical colleges.  However, it was
pointed  out time and again that these norms need to be implemented stringently and objectively.   Besides that, some
reservations were also voiced about the practicability of some of the norms, like requirement of minimum land specially
for hilly, tribal and metropolitan  areas, very high amount of bank guarantee, requirement of infrastructure in the
medical college/teaching hospital etc.    The Committee recommends that  the MCI should undertake an exercise for
reviewing the various norms so as to  examine their viability in the present scenario and bringing  about necessary
modifications therein without compromising the quality.
4.3       The Committee finds that a detailed framework  for starting a new medical college has been  laid down in the
IMC Act, 1956 and the Regulations made thereunder.   The Committee has been given to understand that the formal
permission for starting a new medical college given by the Central Govt on the recommendation of the MCI  includes a
time-bound programme for the establishment of the medical college and expansion of the hospital facilities.  A clear cut
definition of preliminary  requirements to be met in respect of buildings, infrastructural facilities, medical and allied
equipment, faculty and staff etc. before admitting the 1
st batch of  students is also included in the permission, alongwith
annual  targets to be achieved to commensurate with the intake of students during the following years.   The Committee
was also informed that this permission is granted initially for a period of one year to be renewed on yearly basis subject
to verification of the achievements, annual targets and revalidation of the performance bank guarantees.
4.4       It can be said that with  the final authority vested in the Central Govt and MCI, mushrooming of medical
colleges leading to regional imbalance and commercialization of medical education has been checked considerably.  
However,  the Committee observes that there are certain practical problems also which go against the student interest.  
There are instances where medical college once started is not able to  fulfill the commitments made at the initial stage,
thereby losing recognition and thus playing with the future of students enrolled in that college.   The Committee is of the
view that there is a need for building up a mechanism whereby maximum standards are to be met at the very
beginning.   Reports are there where college is started on the basis of Essentiality Certificate and conditional approval.  
However, in the very second year, conditions are not met.    In such a scenario, either the college is allowed to function
so as to safeguard the interest of students or students are shifted to a recognized medical college.   Both the situations
cannot  be considered to be desirable and this should not be allowed to happen.
4.5       The Committee is, therefore, of the view that both the Central Govt. and MCI should have a more cautious
approach while giving approval for a new medical college.   There is a need for assessing  the background of a  trust,
specially its involvement in medical field and non-commercial approach before grant of any permission.   The
Committee, therefore, recommends that definition of the term ‘trust’ should be incorporated in the relevant provisions of
the IMC Act, 1956.

4.6       The Committee has been given to understand that a general view of the requirement of medical manpower is
taken by the State Govts  while providing for establishing a new medical college.   The prescribed form of Essentiality 
Certificate included in the  Establishment of Medical Colleges Regulations, 1999 requires the State Govts to indicate
details of existing medical manpower in the State, doctor-population ratio in the State and the justification for  opening
of the proposed medical college.
4.7       The Committee is not inclined to agree with the view of the Department that although it is necessary to have an
All India assessment of medical manpower requirement, it cannot be made a  pre-condition for starting a new college.  
The Committee strongly feels that the responsibility of the Central Govt does not end with the production of Essentiality
Certificate by State Govt.   The  Committee would like to refer to Sub-Section (7) of Section 10A of the IMC Act, 1956
which deals with recommendation of the Council and approval/disapproval by Central  Govt. for opening of a new
college.   One of the factors to be considered as enumerated in clause (f) is the requirement of manpower in the field of
practice of medicine.   The Committee is, therefore, of the view that both Central and the State Govts should specifically
ensure whether there is a requirement in the  real sense for establishing a medical college in a particular area before
giving its approval for the same.

5.3       During the  course of extensive discussions  with various medical functionaries, several reservations were
pointed out about the inspections carried out by MCI teams from time to time.   The main drawback cited was that the
inspection procedure was not fool-proof and lacked transparency.   General observation was that in majority of medical
colleges, required  staff as per MCI norms did not exist, infrastructure was totally inadequate, there was no proper
building and clinical material was much less than what was required.  At the time of inspection, cover up exercise was
generally carried out.    Reservations were also voiced about very high rate of inspection fee specially in the case of
Govt. medical colleges due to their lack of financial resources.
5.4       The Committee notes that a number of steps  have been taken by MCI to make the procedure of inspection
foolproof.   For example, the medical colleges are now supposed to maintain a list of teachers on their strength 
alongwith their photographs  duly verified by the Dean of the College.    The Committee, however, is of the view that
there is a need for  streamlining the inspection procedure so as to make it more stringent and effective.  The Committee
understands that so far inspections are being carried out only  after giving prior  notice.   The Committee is of the view
that MCI should initiate measures  so as to build up  a  mechanism for carrying out surprise inspections and inspections
at a very short notice.   This would indirectly lead to a  situation where medical college authorities would work towards
having a proper set up as per the prescribed norms.   The Committee is also of  the view that rate  of fees charged  for
different  categories of inspection should be reviewed.   Specially, in spite of   the so-called annual inspections being 
carried out only once in five years,  annual fee of Rs. 30,000 is prescribed  which  seems to be on the high side.

that such developments defeat the very purpose of carrying out an inspection.   The Committee, therefore, strongly
